title: Popular GLP-1 weight-loss drugs linked to potentially deadly brain disorder
summary: A study linked 15 cases of Wernicke encephalopathy to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Mounjaro, raising concerns about vitamin B1 deficiency risks.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss a recent University of California San Diego study regarding the effects of GLP-1 weight loss medication on the biological aging process. Siegel outlines the potential cardiovascular and neurological benefits of the drug while noting side effects related to digestion and thyroid function.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications.

A new study, published in Clinical Nutrition, identified 15 reported cases of Wernicke encephalopathy, a neurological disorder caused by severe vitamin B1 deficiency, in people taking GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Most of the reported cases involved semaglutide, sold under the brand names Ozempic and Wegovy, or tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound.
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS
Researchers found 15 cases through the FDA's Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), published medical literature and their own medical center.
Most patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition, the study noted.
Researchers are warning about a rare but potentially life-threatening brain condition that may be linked to popular GLP-1 weight-loss medications. (iStock)

Reports of the disorder appeared more often among people taking GLP-1 medications than among those taking other drugs, the researchers found. They emphasized, however, that the study cannot prove the medications caused the condition.

Vitamin B1 plays an important role in brain function, the researchers said. Severe deficiencies can cause confusion, trouble walking, balance problems and vision changes. If left untreated, the condition can lead to permanent neurological damage or death.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Karthik Achari, a Chicago-based clinician and founder of PepMD who was not involved in the study, said the findings should be viewed in perspective.

"Researchers went through adverse event reports and the medical literature and found a small number of cases, 15, of Wernicke encephalopathy in people taking GLP-1 drugs," Achari told Fox News Digital. "That's out of millions of people on these medications. So this is rare."
Researchers identified 15 cases, finding that most patients experienced gastrointestinal symptoms or nutritional issues, including weight loss, vomiting, loss of appetite or malnutrition. (iStock)
"But it's real, it's serious, and the mechanism makes sense," he added.
GLP-1 medications can reduce appetite while also causing nausea and vomiting, making it easier for some people to become deficient in vitamin B1, Achari said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"The drug shrinks your appetite. It doesn't shrink your body's requirements," he said. "You can now eat very little without feeling it, which is the point of the medication, but your need for protein, vitamins, and fluids didn't go anywhere."

People with persistent nausea and vomiting, those losing weight very quickly while eating little, people with a history of bariatric surgery and those who use alcohol heavily may face a higher risk, Achari said.
The medications suppress appetite, experts say, but the body's requirements for nutrients and hydration remain the same. (iStock)
Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," said proper nutrition and hydration should be considered part of treatment while taking GLP-1 medications.

"GLP-1 medications can dramatically reduce appetite, but that also means people may unintentionally under-eat the very things their bodies need most, especially protein, fiber and fluids," she told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Palinski-Wade said ongoing vomiting or diarrhea can increase the risk of dehydration and kidney problems. She urged patients to seek medical guidance if those symptoms continue for roughly 24 hours.
"Don't assume every side effect is just part of being on a GLP-1," Palinski-Wade said. "Severe or persistent symptoms deserve attention."

The researchers acknowledged that the study relied largely on reports submitted to the FDA and cannot prove GLP-1 medications caused the condition. They called for additional research, and experts said patients should not stop taking prescribed GLP-1 medications based on these findings alone.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and the researchers for comment.
Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Food divorce’ trend among couples could drive them apart, experts warn
summary: The "food divorce" trend has some couples eating separately, but experts warn the growing trend erodes relationship quality and emotional well-being over time.
story: Regularly splitting apart for meals may contribute to isolation and disconnection, according to dietitian Tanya Freirich. Sharing flexible, modular meals can make it easier for people with different needs or schedules to eat together.

Between differing diet plans, food intolerances and conflicting work schedules, some couples are choosing "food divorce," a term circulating on social media for partners who intentionally cook, order and eat their meals separately.
While taking separate paths at mealtime might solve logistical headaches, experts warn that splitting up at the dinner table can come at a cost to the relationship.
Shared family meals can help people reconnect, build stronger emotional bonds and reduce stress, according to health institutions like Mayo Clinic.
‘QUIET QUITTING’ IN MARRIAGE: THE SUBTLE SIGNS A SPOUSE HAS EMOTIONALLY CHECKED OUT
For couples, experts say regularly eating apart could become a concern if it reflects broader emotional distance or reduces opportunities to spend meaningful time together.
Nutrition experts emphasize the issue is often less about the food itself and more about the lost opportunity for a built-in daily checkpoint.
"Food divorce" refers to the growing trend of couples intentionally cooking, ordering and eating meals separately due to conflicting schedules or specialized diets. (iStock)
"I think it reflects many people's very busy schedules," Tanya Freirich, a North Carolina-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital.

"Mealtime can be a time to unite, to communicate, to build social relationships and foster a connection," she said. "If we're eating completely alone or at different times than important people in our lives, it may foster a little bit of disconnection."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Eating separately can contribute to a "roommate dynamic," experts note. Without regular time to reconnect and discuss the day, couples may have fewer opportunities for communication.
The practice can also contribute to isolation, according to Freirich.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes," she said.
"If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for mental health or well-being."

Eating alone can contribute to isolation, an expert warned. "If so many Americans are eating every meal alone for many days or most of their days, that certainly can't be great for our mental health or well-being." (iStock)
There can also be practical drawbacks because preparing separate meals or ordering from different restaurants may increase grocery costs, preparation time and kitchen cleanup.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Additionally, eating solo can affect individual dietary habits. Studies show people dining alone are more likely to eat quickly, mindlessly scroll on their phones or settle for heavily processed convenience foods compared to when they share meals with others.
"Communities all around the world for thousands of years have come together around mealtimes."
Couples can accommodate different dietary needs without preparing entirely separate meals.
For those navigating specific calorie targets, plant-based diets or medical restrictions, Freirich recommended building "modular" or "choose your own adventure" meals as a more efficient method.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Something like a deconstructed taco night, grain bowls, a pasta or noodle night or even a sheet pan meal where you're creating each food on its own," the expert said.
"So the protein, the carb, the veggies are being cooked separately. And then you get to decide your portions and make your own meal from those ingredients that can meet everyone's needs."
Research highlights that nearly one in four Americans eats every meal alone on any given day, increasing the risk of isolation. (iStock)
When conflicting schedules or caregiving duties make daily dinners impossible, experts recommend prioritizing quality over frequency.
Even sharing a quick weekend breakfast or setting aside one designated night a week can help maintain connection.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Be very intentional to connect when you can," Freirich suggested.
"Make that a really special meal. Be intentional with your connection. Put the phone away, and actually enjoy the other person's company."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Nighttime bathroom trips could reveal hidden health issues — here's when to worry
summary: Nocturia affects half of adults over 50, but experts say frequent nighttime urination could signal sleep apnea, diabetes or an enlarged prostate.
story: Dr. Wendy Troxel shares why getting the recommended amount of nightly shuteye doesn't always leave people refreshed, and outlines the most common reasons for poor sleep quality.
Getting out of bed once during the night to use the bathroom is common, but repeated trips could signal underlying issues, health experts warn.

Waking up more than once a night to urinate can meet the clinical definition of nocturia, which affects about half of adults over 50 and becomes more common with age, according to a recent StudyFinds report. The International Continence Society’s formal definition of nocturia includes even one nighttime trip, but frequency, disruption and a change from a person’s usual pattern all matter.

"Everyone has a baseline of what’s normal urinary frequency for them," Dr. Ali Dabaja, a urologist at Henry Ford Health in Michigan, told the outlet. "But if you wake at least twice to go to the bathroom during eight hours of sleep, that’s considered nocturia."
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID
Nocturia isn't simply a bladder issue, according to Dr. Jeffrey Chester, a licensed physician and medical director of The Ohana Luxury Addiction Treatment Center in Hawaii.

"A change in nighttime urinary patterns is definitely worth mentioning to a physician or healthcare provider, especially when it begins suddenly, becomes more frequent, or disrupts a person's sleep," Chester told Fox News Digital.
Nighttime bathroom trips can disrupt sleep and may become more common with age. (iStock)
Alcohol and caffeine intake, the amount and timing of fluid consumption, and certain medications can all contribute, he added.
Waking up once isn't a cause for concern, agreed Catherine Darley, a naturopathic doctor and founder of Skilled Sleeper in Seattle.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
But more than once can be "concerning," she told Fox News Digital.

Experts note that it can raise the risk of falls, especially for those with mobility or balance challenges. Research shows two or more nightly trips to the bathroom are linked to a higher risk of fall-related injuries, StudyFinds reported.
Repeated nighttime wake-ups to use the bathroom can increase fall risks, research has found. (iStock)
Sleep disorders can also be a factor, Darley said, including obstructive sleep apnea, which can affect hormones involved in suppressing urine production overnight.
Restless legs syndrome could also contribute to nighttime urination and is more common with age, Darley added.
OLDER ADULTS TAKING 5 OR MORE PRESCRIPTION DRUGS FACE HIGHER RISK OF DEATH, STUDY FINDS
She advised starting with your primary care provider to look for an underlying cause, and checking in with doctors and pharmacists to see if medications could be involved in frequent bathroom trips.
In some cases, they could adjust the timing to prevent late-night wake-ups.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Other issues could be the cause, too, according to StudyFinds, including diabetes, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate and fluid buildup.
Experts say the timing and amount of fluids, caffeine, alcohol and some medications can contribute to nighttime urination. (iStock)
For some people, simple habits can help, including not drinking for roughly two hours before bedtime and stopping alcohol about three hours before bed, Darley said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

She also suggested keeping floors clear of rugs and clutter, using gentle amber lighting, sitting on the edge of the bed before standing to avoid getting dizzy — and installing grab bars for extra support.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Political fights can rip couples apart — therapist shares 3 ways to save a relationship
summary: A marriage therapist reveals three strategies for couples navigating the political divide, from setting boundaries to finding compromise.
story: Dr. Anna Elton discusses why partisan disagreements can create tension between partners, and offers strategies for setting boundaries, staying curious and reconnecting after heated conversations.
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research – and experts say those divisions may also be straining some marriages.

Some high-profile couples, including Democratic strategist James Carville and his wife, Republican political consultant Mary Matalin, have remained together despite their differing views – but experts say navigating those differences isn't always easy.
Anna Elton, Ph.D., a licensed marriage and family therapist and clinical sexologist in Massachusetts, said she has counseled couples on different sides of the political aisle.
'QUIET QUITTING' COULD SILENTLY DESTROY YOUR MARRIAGE – 4 WAYS TO BRING THE SPARK BACK
"A lot of couples come in and they want to work on communication, and politics can come up in our sessions," Elton, author of "The Formula of Desire," told Fox News Digital.
"I work with a number of couples who are in this place where they have a family, they have kids, but they can't talk about politics."
More than one-third of Americans report having ended a relationship over political differences, according to recent research. (iStock)
For many singles, Elton said, political compatibility is now something they consider early in the dating process.
WHY COUPLES SHOULD FLIRT WITH EACH OTHER EVERY DAY – PLUS THE 'RED FLAG' TO AVOID
She referenced a recent study that found younger adults tend to make assumptions about religion, gender roles, empathy and other characteristics based on political affiliation.
"So, before you get to know the person, you’ve already created this assumption of who this person is."
Younger daters are more likely to choose who they want to date based on political affiliation, experts say. (iStock)

"I've definitely been hearing from my younger clients who are saying, ‘I want to know which political party this person belongs to, and then I'll see if I want to even be going on a date and wasting my time with this person.’"
COMMON MARRIAGE HABIT COULD QUIETLY KILL YOUR SEX LIFE, EXPERT WARNS
For couples who have been married for decades, today's political divisions may present challenges that didn't exist when their relationships began, Elton noted.
The expert offered the following three tips for navigating politically charged conversations with a partner in a healthy way.
No. 1: Set boundaries ahead of time
Come up with rules for the conversation and set the tone before it starts, Elton suggested, noting that the first three minutes of a discussion typically predict the outcome.
Conversations that begin with a harsh tone or accusatory language are unlikely to be productive, she said. "So, before you talk, say, ‘OK, these are our boundaries for this conversation.’"
The first three minutes of a discussion can typically predict the outcome, according to the expert. (iStock)
Those boundaries can also extend to media habits, Elton said, including limiting how much political content couples consume, especially on social media.

"You read certain things and then all of a sudden, you keep scrolling on your social media and you see similar content coming up over and over and over again," Elton said. "And at this point, it creates an illusionary effect."
HOW OFTEN ARE MARRIED PEOPLE HAVING SEX? WHAT TO KNOW ABOUT THE INTIMACY STANDARD IN AMERICA

Hearing the same information repeatedly may lead people to gradually accept it as true, according to Elton. "Now think about two people who are in their echo chambers, and they're exposed to certain information that is contradicting each other."

As a general rule, Elton said couples should be mindful not to spend more time on their phones than they do engaging with each other. Excessive screen time can reduce face-to-face connection, leaving less room for eye contact, conversation and other shared experiences.
Set boundaries regarding how much political content you consume, especially when with your partner, the expert advised. (iStock)
Also, when someone is constantly consuming political content, it can become the primary topic they want to discuss, creating tension when partners hold different views, she cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

To help reduce conflict, Elton recommended limiting when political news or posts are consumed. She also suggested setting aside one phone-free date night each week to encourage face-to-face connection.
No. 2: Agree to disagree
While couples with differing political views are unlikely to agree on every issue, "agreeing to disagree" can help prevent hostility.
"We can still love each other," Elton said. "It's not going to affect our relationship."

"As soon as it gets to the point of seeing your partner through the lens of ‘if you believe this, this is who you are, and I can’t believe that I'm still in a relationship with you,’ that becomes a problem."
When political beliefs become the defining feature of a partner, relationships can suffer, according to the expert. (iStock)

Elton urged couples not to take political disagreements personally and instead approach them with curiosity. She also recommended looking at the same information together, allowing each partner to ask questions and draw their own conclusions rather than jumping into a heated debate.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The therapist also encouraged couples to focus on areas of common ground rather than viewing disagreements in black-and-white terms.
After a disagreement or failure to compromise, it’s important to always reconnect with your partner, she emphasized.
Never end a fight without re-connecting, the therapist advised. (iStock)
Sharing reassuring words like "I love you" and "You matter to me more than anything else" can be helpful, she said.
"I feel like you always need to say, ‘Hey, I hear what you're saying, but I'm not agreeing, and that's OK.’"
3. Consider the wider impact
When politics come into play in a relationship, it can have an impact on more than just the couple.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Elton encouraged partners to consider how sharing certain opinions can impact other loved ones, especially if one person confides in a family member or friend about the other's views.
"You can create this triangulation where you're connecting with someone against your partner, and you don't want that," she warned.

"Talk to your therapist, vent to your therapist… because if you start venting to your family and friends, then they start forming certain opinions about your partner, and it can affect how they talk to them, how they interact with them."
Before making any drastic decisions, such as ending a relationship over political discord, Elton suggested slowing down and returning to a more grounded state.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We hear certain things and we fill in the gaps," she said. "When we hear someone's political affiliation, we often make assumptions about who they are without really hearing them out."
Rather than making assumptions based on the media or podcasts a partner consumes, for example, Elton encouraged couples to ask questions, stay curious and remain open-minded.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Very hot' coffee and tea linked to higher cancer risk in nearly 1 million adults
summary: A University of Oxford study of nearly 1 million adults links very hot tea and coffee to a threefold higher risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
story: Dr. Aaron Sasson, chief of surgical oncology at Stony Brook Cancer Center in New York, confirmed that drinking hot beverages or drinking hot liquids can irritate the esophagus, which could contribute to the development of esophageal cancer.
Regularly drinking very hot tea or coffee may raise the risk of a type of esophageal cancer, according to a large study at the University of Oxford.

People who reported drinking beverages "very hot" had about three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), a type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the esophagus, compared to those who drank warm beverages.

Drinking six or more hot drinks per day was associated with a 71% higher risk of the disease. The same link was not seen for esophageal adenocarcinoma (AC), a type of cancer that develops in the lower part of the esophagus.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND

The study included nearly 1 million U.K. adults, making it the largest investigation of its kind to date, according to lead study author Keren Papier, a nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford.

Roughly half of the participants were from the Million Women Study (MWS), who were followed for an average of 14 years, and the other half were from the UK Biobank (UKB), who were followed for 11 years.
Regularly drinking very hot tea or coffee may raise the risk of a type of esophageal cancer, according to a large study at the University of Oxford. (iStock)

"Compared with people who reported drinking their beverages ‘warm,’ those who drank them ‘hot’ had around a 1.7 times higher risk of SCC, while those who drank them ‘very hot’ had around a three times higher risk," Papier told Fox News Digital.
The study was published in the International Journal of Cancer.
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

The researchers estimated that, if the observed association reflects a true cause-and-effect relationship, about 14% of SCC cases could potentially be prevented if people drank beverages "hot" rather than "very hot."

The biggest limitation, according to the researchers, is that beverage temperatures were self-reported rather than directly measured. Because people's tolerance for heat differs, participants may have classified similar temperatures differently.
"If you are a heavy consumer of hot tea or coffee, maybe you'd want to cool it down a little bit."

"A limitation of our study was that, although we examined associations by self-reported preferred drink temperature, we did not have data on directly measured drink temperatures, and, therefore, cannot determine how self-reported drink temperature is likely to relate to absolute drink temperature," Papier noted.
"These findings don't mean people need to stop drinking tea or coffee. Just let your drinks cool down a little before drinking them."

People who reported drinking beverages "very hot" had about three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, a type of cancer that begins in the cells lining the esophagus, compared to those who drank warm beverages. (iStock)
An outside cancer specialist agreed the findings are biologically plausible but said they should be interpreted in context.

Dr. Aaron Sasson, chief of surgical oncology and co-director of the gastrointestinal oncology team at Stony Brook Cancer Center in New York, said it’s been known that drinking hot beverages or liquids can be irritating to the esophagus and that it could contribute to the development of esophageal cancer.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The hotter the liquid, the higher the risk of a "thermal injury," the doctor told Fox News Digital.

"Similar to burning your hand, if you were to get a burn on your hand, you have an increased risk of getting squamous cell carcinoma of the hand, of the skin developing in the burned area," Sasson said. "So, think of that as constantly repeating a burn to the esophagus."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The doctor reiterated that this study specifically looked at the risk of squamous carcinomas, not adenocarcinomas.
"In the United States, about 85% of all of our cancers are adenocarcinomas. So, the incidence of squamous carcinomas in the esophagus is quite low, just to put it into perspective," he noted.
The hotter the liquid, the higher the risk of a "thermal injury," a doctor told Fox News Digital. (iStock)
The lifetime risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus in the U.S. is less than 1%, the doctor said.
Sasson agreed that there was no "objective measurement" of the drinks’ temperature, which poses an unknown variable.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If you are a heavy consumer of hot tea or coffee, maybe you'd want to cool it down a little bit," he advised. "But I think, for practical purposes, for most people, [it’s] not the predominant risk factor for squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Smoking, heavy alcohol use, acid reflux and obesity are among the better-established risk factors for esophageal cancer, Sasson said.
"If you were to limit alcohol consumption and eliminate cigarette smoking, you will have done wonders for your esophagus."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Son who lost father in 9/11 attacks shares powerful lessons 25 years later: ‘I’m still here’
summary: A 9/11 survivor's son reveals the grief techniques that transformed his mental health 25 years after losing his father at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.
story: Grief podcaster David Ferrugio, author of "You’re Not Dead Yet," reflects on losing his dad in the Sept. 11 attacks and why hearing others’ experiences has reshaped his outlook.
As the nation marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, the weight of the loss of loved ones still looms.
Podcaster David Ferrugio, author of the new book "You're Not Dead Yet," joined Fox News Digital to discuss how his own grief persists 25 years after 9/11.
The host of the "DEAD Talks" podcast lost his father, David Frances Ferrugio, who worked at the World Trade Center, in the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
GROUND ZERO FIRST RESPONDER NEEDED MAJOR SURGERY DECADES AFTER 9/11 EXPOSURE: 'I THOUGHT IT WAS OVER'
Ferrugio, who was 12 years old and living in New Jersey at the time, recalls watching television footage of the towers collapsing and "breaking down."

"It was like a dividing moment in my memory and my life, because I was one person on September 11th, and then on September 12th, it was a whole new reality I walked into, which inspired what I'm doing."
Podcaster David Ferrugio lost his father in the 9/11 attacks when he was 12 years old. (David Ferrugio)
After years of internalizing his emotions, Ferrugio discovered the power of sharing stories of grief.
On his podcast, he invites guests to discuss their own experiences with death and loss.
MAN TURNS TRAGIC LOSS OF BEST FRIEND TO SUICIDE INTO URGENT OUTREACH TO LONELY STRANGERS
"Eventually, I got comfortable expressing myself and learning the importance of just sharing [my] story and telling people how I feel and opening up," he said.
Drawing from his own experiences, Ferrugio shares several lessons that have helped him navigate grief.
No. 1: Embrace the uncomfortable

Although discussions of grief can be difficult, even decades after a traumatic event like 9/11, Ferrugio said "embracing the uncomfortable" and talking it out is "an important piece of this complex puzzle."
Sharing stories of loss can provide emotional release while also helping others feel less alone, he noted, adding that he's seen firsthand how those conversations can make a difference.
According to Ferrugio, it’s important to allow for moments of joy, even during times of grief. (David Ferrugio)
"Even when I have my days of just not feeling it, I'm reminded by the people who reach out and the way they share their story ... how much it is impacting so many people."
Finding a sense of community can be especially meaningful at a time when so many people are experiencing loneliness, whether they're grieving or not, Ferrugio added.
FAITH CAN BRING HEALING 25 YEARS AFTER SEPTEMBER 11 TRAGEDY, PASTOR SAYS
"I've learned so much through the eyes of others, and I think the storytelling is just so vital."
Fear of judgment often keeps people from sharing their stories, even though doing so can bring a sense of "liberation," according to Ferrugio.
As the nation marks 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, the loss of loved ones still weighs heavily.  (iStock)
No. 2: Embrace a new perspective
More than two decades after the attacks, Ferrugio shared that his mental health has improved after putting in "a lot of effort," including shifting his perspective on life and death.
"Life and death are the same coin, just two different sides – and there's a thin veil between them," he said.

"It’s completely shifted the way I live my life through seeing what other people are going through ... understanding the pain people are experiencing, how they manage it ... how they reframe it, and understanding that as alone as this life can feel, we're not as alone as we think."
"It's important to zoom out and realize, ‘I've done this for 25 years, and I'm still here.'"
Grief can reshape how people approach life, Ferrugio said, encouraging them to be more present, embrace the full range of emotions and give themselves grace, even during life's most difficult times.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Ultimately, all these conversations I've had are conversations about grief, but they're really conversations about how we can live this life."
No. 3: Breathe
When painful emotions or a wave of grief start to roll in, Ferrugio's go-to technique is to allow himself to feel it and "breathe it out."
"A lot of breath work works wonders for me," he said. "A deep breath is going to do more for you than you think."
Along with breath work, Ferrugio said exercising and spending time in nature have helped calm his nervous system, noting that what works best varies from person to person.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"We forget to look inward, and we all have that intuition and that guttural feeling – we have to trust what we're saying to ourselves," he said. "What feels good? Does this feel like it's working?"
No. 4: Find light in the dark
It’s important to allow for moments of joy, even during times of grief, said Ferrugio.

"Give yourself permission to feel moments of levity, to feel moments of joy, even if it is for five seconds. … Just take those moments and cherish them, because the contrast of the joy and pain exists for a reason."
Two flags flutter on a fence in front of Lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

"It's not easy to feel however you feel, but it takes a lot of effort and discomfort to try to step out of that. … Whatever we go through in life, it's an ebb and flow, and sometimes both are happening at the same time."
On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Ferrugio acknowledged that the pain of losing his father remains.

"For anyone else who's been part of that day, I just hope they look back at the days they've gone through and see that they're still here," he said.
"You're still with us, and you’re still grinding. You're showing up for the people in your life."

"It's important to zoom out and realize, ‘I've done this for 25 years, and I'm still here.’"

title: Alcohol tied to surprising cancer death pattern in adults under 55, researchers find
summary: Alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in the United States more than doubled from 1990 to 2023, with colorectal cancer surpassing liver cancer in younger men.
story: A University of Miami cancer expert reveals why alcohol is an increasingly important modifiable cancer risk factor, including its potential role in colorectal cancer among younger men.

Annual U.S. cancer deaths tied to alcohol consumption more than doubled over a three-decade period, according to a recent study led by researchers at the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.

The findings, published in The Lancet Regional Health — Americas and presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting in Chicago, revealed that alcohol-attributable cancer deaths jumped from 11,361 in 1990 to 23,126 in 2023.
Researchers analyzed more than 30 years of data from the Global Burden of Disease study to track the trends.
BEER, WINE OR LIQUOR? MASSIVE STUDY REVEALS WHICH WAS LINKED TO LOWER DEATH RISK
While alcohol has long been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, surveys show that awareness of its link to cancer remains limited.

"The most surprising finding was the breadth of alcohol’s potential impact across cancer types," Chinmay Jani, M.D., corresponding author of the study and chief fellow in hematology and oncology at Sylvester, told Fox News Digital.
The study highlights that liquor may have a different risk profile than wine despite containing similar amounts of alcohol. (iStock)

"Although its relationship with liver cancer is widely recognized, its contribution to cancers such as colorectal, esophageal, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer is less understood by the public."
CANCER DOCTOR REVEALS 5 HABITS THAT MAY REDUCE DISEASE RISK AND IMPROVE OUTCOMES

The research showed that older adults and men bore the highest overall burden of alcohol-related cancer deaths. Among older men, liver cancer was the primary cause of alcohol-attributable mortality, followed closely by esophageal and colorectal cancers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found.

Among younger adults between the ages of 20 and 54, colorectal cancer emerged as the leading cause of alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in men and the second leading cause in women, surpassing liver cancer in both groups.
Breast cancer was the leading cause of alcohol-related cancer deaths among women overall, the study found. (iStock)

The authors noted that the findings carry significant weight for public health messaging, particularly because general awareness surrounding alcohol's connection to various cancers remains low compared to known risks like tobacco use.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Because no minimum "safe" level of alcohol has been established, researchers said drinking less may help lower long-term cancer risk.
Because the study used existing national data rather than following individuals over time, researchers couldn’t determine each person’s exact drinking habits or account for every lifestyle factor.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As a result, the findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit.
The findings show a strong association between alcohol use and cancer deaths, but they cannot prove that alcohol directly caused those deaths or establish a specific "safe" drinking limit. (iStock)

"What this study makes clear is that alcohol-related cancer risk is not limited to one disease or one group of people," Gilberto Lopes, M.D., senior author and chief of the Division of Medical Oncology at the Miller School, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"As physicians and cancer researchers, we have an opportunity to help patients understand that alcohol is a modifiable risk factor and that even small, informed changes can be part of a broader strategy to reduce cancer risk in our community."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Ground Zero first responder needed major surgery decades after 9/11 exposure: ‘I thought it was over’
summary: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky shares how Ground Zero dust exposure led to years of hospitalizations, steroids and a rare airway disease diagnosis.
story: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky and an NYU doctor share how exposure to World Trade Center dust can have serious health consequences decades later.
Those who were present at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2001, continue to experience the physical effects of their exposure.
As Lower Manhattan was engulfed in dust and debris from the remnants of both towers, first responders and survivors were forced to breathe in toxic air.

More than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, physical-injury risks and stressful conditions in the days, weeks and months following the attacks, according to the World Trade Center Health Program.
SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING

As of March 2025, 8,215 people who had enrolled in the WTC Health Program had died, including 5,844 responders, as reported by the CDC. The figures include deaths from all causes; the program does not track whether a member’s death was related to 9/11 exposure.
A responder’s long-term health battle
In an interview with Fox News Digital, Mordechai Shedrowitzky, a volunteer EMT who responded on 9/11, shared how his exposure led to multiple hospitalizations and, ultimately, major surgery.

FDNY firefighters and rescue workers attend to an injured firefighter in the rubble of the World Trade Center in Manhattan, New York, after it was destroyed by planes in a terrorist attack on Sept. 11, 2001. (Getty Images)

Queens-born Shedrowitzky, 51, was living in Brooklyn at the time of the attacks. After helping cover his local area for much of the day, he headed into Lower Manhattan that evening to assist with the response.

"My most vivid memory was actually entering Manhattan from Brooklyn," he said. "As we approached the tunnel, the first thing we noticed was there were no lights, there was no electricity in the area, it [was] pitch black."
FOX NEWS' ERIC SHAWN REVEALS CANCER AND RESPIRATORY ILLNESS FROM 9/11 TOXIC DUST
"When we entered the tunnel, there was a tremendous amount of swirling debris, at speeds that I just can't even imagine."
Once Shedrowitzky and his team arrived at South Street Seaport, where his ambulance was staged with others, he described the debris as "overwhelming."
"I remember the engine actually sputtering at times," he said. "I would imagine that it was taking in a tremendous amount of dust."
Firefighters gather near ground zero after the attack on the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. (Corbis via Getty Images)

"We were definitely not cognizant of what effect ... the air might have on us. And therefore, we did spend a significant amount of time outside of the ambulances, just commiserating with the people around us."
Shedrowitzky said he "thought it was over" once he left the scene. But years later, he noticed small symptoms that were turning into a big problem.
His pre-existing asthma — which typically flared during seasonal changes and caused coughing that required an inhaler — was worsening each year.
AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK

"I started to require oral steroids," he said. "I would have wheezing; I would have coughing. It would last longer; it would be more serious ... I wouldn't be able to go to work, wouldn’t be able to take care of my kids. So, the effects were definitely increasing over time."
Shedrowitzky added that his condition was "getting to the point where it was leading to frequent respiratory infections and hospitalizations."
A graphic shows a close-up of dust particles breathed in during the 9/11 terrorist attacks. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
In 2019, Shedrowitzky described that his condition got "significantly worse," after experiencing a cough that wouldn’t resolve itself, even after the "highest doses" of steroids and antibiotics.
NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11
Shedrowitzky ultimately was put in touch with the World Trade Center Health Program – a federal program administered by the CDC – where his condition was classified as 9/11-related and was monitored.
It was eventually confirmed that Shedrowitzky had tracheobronchomalacia, a condition in which the walls of the windpipe and major airways weaken and collapse during breathing.
Mordechai Shedrowitzky and Dr. Denise Harrison of NYU Langone's WTC Health Program are pictured on Sept. 8, 2026. (Khloe Quill/Fox News Digital)
"[It] was probably secondary to both the asthma getting worse as well as steroid use over the years to try to treat those symptoms," he said.
In 2024, Shedrowitzky underwent a procedure called a tracheobronchoplasty to structurally reinforce his trachea and main bronchi.
RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA
Two years after the procedure, he said he is feeling "much better," although he still experiences occasional infections. He hopes to return to work as a physical therapist soon.
"Even a couple of months ago, I wouldn't have been able to speak for more than a very short time," Shedrowitzky said.
"It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11."
As a father of six, Shedrowitzky – who is now also a grandfather of two – said his condition made it difficult for him to spend time with his children as they were growing up.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Things as simple as lifting my children, even speaking to them," he said. "The amount of time that I spent in the hospital and its effect on them was quite significant."
"Now, they're older, but my ability to spend time, interact with them ... has been greatly improved."
Treating 9/11-related illnesses
Dr. Denise Harrison, medical director of the NYU Grossman School of Medicine WTC Health Program Clinical Center of Excellence, has been involved in post-9/11 healthcare since 2002.
The program has since grown to provide screening, monitoring and treatment for people experiencing health effects related to their 9/11 exposure.
The doctor noted that the dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways.
People rush away from the collapsing World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, after two hijacked airplanes hit the twin towers in New York City in a terrorist attack. (Getty Images)

"Usually, the larger size dust gets deposited in the upper airways and the smaller size dust gets deposited in the lower airways," she told Fox News Digital. "Because of the overwhelming nature of the disaster, a significant number of large particles got deposited into the lower airways as well. So, this is not just the airways, but also the digestive tract, in the esophagus."

Harrison said patients often report sinus problems, asthma and COPD. These conditions can occur alongside other "aerodigestive" issues, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may complicate diagnosis and treatment.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Other 9/11-related conditions may also be interlinked.
"We have patients with asthma and PTSD who might perceive their asthma symptoms differently than the patients without PTSD, so that requires a combination of providers," the doctor said.
The dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways, the doctor noted. (iStock)
Shedrowitzky urged other first responders who are experiencing health issues to not wait to get help and to confirm that what they’re experiencing may be linked to 9/11.
"Continue to be monitored so that potential issues can be picked up early," he advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"If we can look back and see the quality of life that it's robbing you of, it might push you to contact the World Trade Center Health Program, get the help that you need."
NYU Langone's WTC Health Program 9/11 exhibit is on display. (Angelica Stabile/Fox News Digital)
As of March 31, 2025, the WTC Health Program had more than 130,000 currently enrolled members.
The program, which is authorized through 2090, operates branches across multiple health systems, including NYU Langone Health, Mount Sinai, Northwell, Stony Brook and Rutgers.

Harrison reiterated that the health effects of 9/11 exposure remain "persistent," and can be exacerbated by the environment and other illnesses. Experts predict that the fallout will continue for decades to come.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Symptoms are still ongoing and research is still ongoing," she said, urging the public and responders to "have patience."
"While it might not directly benefit them or may provide some benefits now, it could be more beneficial in the future and help the overall response to disasters."
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Weight regain after obesity drugs tied to higher odds of suicidal thoughts in observational study
summary: Weight-loss drug users who regained weight had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation, according to a study analyzing data from over 27,000 adults.
story: Bonnie Mitchell, a licensed professional clinical counselor in California, said that while a new study shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, it cannot prove causation.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study.
The research, conducted at Asan Medical Center in South Korea, analyzed data from 27,741 adults (10,908 men and 16,833 women).
Of these participants, 846 had been taking prescription medications for weight control during the previous year, while 26,895 did not take them.
OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS
The weight-loss drug users were 1.9 times more likely to experience depression and twice as likely to seek mental health counseling.
They were also 2.7 times more likely to have suicidal thoughts and 1.7 times more likely to make a suicide attempt.

Adults who reported using prescription weight-loss medication in the last year had higher rates of depression, mental-health counseling, suicidal thoughts and suicide-related behaviors compared to people who did not take the drugs, according to an observational study. (iStock)
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight.

"The tendency for depression and suicide-related indicators to increase as weight rebounds after using weight-loss drugs may reflect not only the neuropsychiatric effects of the drugs themselves, but also a complex interplay of psychological and social factors associated with failed weight control," the research team wrote in the study.
PATIENTS TAKING WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS OFTEN MAKE 5 CRITICAL MISTAKES, DOCTOR WARNS
The findings were published in the Korean Journal of Family Practice on Aug. 23.
Bonnie Mitchell, doctor of behavioral health and licensed professional clinical counselor in California, noted that this was an observational, cross-sectional study.
The associations were stronger among those using the medications who gained or regained weight. (iStock)

"It shows a correlation between weight-loss drug use and self-reported mental health symptoms, but it cannot prove causation," she told Fox News Digital. "It does not demonstrate that weight-loss medications directly induce depression or suicidal thoughts."
The data was collected between 2013 and 2022.

"During most of this period, modern GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists used for weight loss (such as high-dose semaglutide/Wegovy or tirzepatide/Zepbound/Mounjaro) were either not yet on the market or had very limited real world uptake in South Korea," Mitchell said.
WHEN IS A MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS TOO SEVERE FOR TELEHEALTH? WARNING SIGNS FAMILIES SHOULDN'T IGNORE
"The study sample captures older anti-obesity agents historically prescribed in South Korea during that decade, including phentermine, diethylpropion, phendimetrazine, topiramate and orlistat."
Central nervous system stimulants – including phentermine-based drugs – have been shown to carry risks of anxiety, mood changes and insomnia, the counselor noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to a mental health counselor. (iStock)
"The study highlighted a striking sub finding that found users who gained weight despite taking the medication had 4.2 times higher odds of suicidal ideation compared to non-users," Mitchell noted.
Weight regain or perceived "failure" in weight management can trigger profound guilt, shame, helplessness and psychological distress, according to the expert.

"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia," Mitchell said. "A cross-sectional survey cannot separate pre-existing mental health struggles from new symptoms that arose after starting a medication."
"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care."

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight.
The researchers also need to determine whether mental health risks differ between specific weight-loss drugs.
NEW WEIGHT-LOSS COMPOUND MELTS FAT WITHOUT CURBING APPETITE — AND PRESERVES MUSCLE

"Even though GLP-1 clinical trials show low absolute risk, the FDA’s product labels for chronic weight management drugs (like Wegovy and Zepbound) include warnings to monitor for mood changes," Mitchell noted.

She recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications, evaluating past or current depression, bipolar disorder, or history of suicidal ideation or behavior.

More research is needed to determine whether weight-loss medications themselves affect mental health, or whether depression and other symptoms are related to factors such as obesity or difficulties losing weight. (iStock)
"Individuals with severe obesity have higher baseline rates of depression, anxiety and body dysmorphia."

"Doctors can inform patients and caregivers about potential mood changes so they know what to watch for," Mitchell said. "The next important step for ongoing monitoring would be to schedule check-ins at 4- to 8-week intervals during dose escalation, to evaluate both physiological progress and psychological well-being."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Patients should contact their healthcare provider immediately if they notice new or worsening depressive symptoms, including the following.

Persistent low mood, unexplained sadness or severe fatigueAnhedonia (loss of interest in activities once enjoyed)Increased anxiety, agitation, panic attacks or extreme restlessnessSleep disturbance or insomniaNew or worsening thoughts of self-harm or suicideMarked changes in behavior or personality, reported by friends or family

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Any active suicidal thoughts require immediate emergency medical care," Mitchell advised.
"If a patient develops emergent depression or suicidal ideation during treatment, clinicians should discontinue the weight-loss medication and connect the patient with psychiatric support."
Eli Lilly, manufacturer of the tirzepatide weight-loss medication Zepbound, explicitly mentions "depression or thoughts of suicide" in its safety information.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"You should pay attention to changes in your mood, behaviors, feelings or thoughts," the website reads.
It further advises patients to contact a healthcare provider if mental health changes are "new, worse or worry you."
An expert recommends that a physician conducts a baseline mental health history before prescribing new weight-loss medications. (iStock)
On Lilly's medical-information site, the company says that after reviewing clinical trials and medical reports, "no increased risk" of suicidal ideation or psychiatric adverse effects was identified.

Novo Nordisk, manufacturer of the semaglutide weight-loss medication Wegovy, states in its trials that less than 1% of participants experienced suicidal ideation or behavior during treatment. It also says there was "no difference between semaglutide 2.4 mg and placebo."

title: ‘Trojan horses’ in America: Congress probes influence networks tied to China, Iran and Cuba
summary: Lawmakers will examine alleged foreign malign influence operations tied to China, Iran and Cuba after Fox News Digital traced pro-communist network operating inside the U.S.
story: D.C. CodePink organizer Olivia DiNucci shouted and unfurled a ‘SANCTIONS KILL IN CUBA’ during a panel discussion at the Institute of World Politics on Sept. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C., before security removed her. (Credit: CodePink via Storyful)

Last Tuesday, at the corner of Church Street and 16th Street NW, blocks from the White House, Christine Balling, a former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Command South, led a panel discussion on the national security threat that communist-run Cuba poses to the U.S.

Suddenly, a fresh-faced former college basketball star, Olivia DiNucci, stood up to steal the stage at the Institute of World Politics, yelling as she clutched a hand-painted banner: "SANCTIONS KILL IN CUBA."

"There is global solidarity with Gaza and Cuba and ICE here," DiNucci shouted breathlessly, as security officials grabbed her banner and pushed her out a side door as she kept yelling, "because the liberation of our people is rooted in our neighbors!"
In small print, the banner had DiNucci's organizational and ideological affiliation: "CODEPINK."

DiNucci is a D.C.-based political organizer with CodePink, a left-wing political agitation group, spending her days and evenings as a professional protester and a regular gadfly, disrupting dinners, hearings and conferences as a sidekick to CodePink co-founder Susan Medea Benjamin. Their group supports the Communist Party of Cuba and has led caravans to the island nation, as Treasury Department officials investigate whether they violated any laws barring Americans from doing business with the communist regime.

For Balling and her co-panelist, Michael Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation and a Cuban American firmly opposed to the communist government of Cuba, DiNucci's political theater wasn't the benign act of an "anti-war" group, as CodePink describes itself.
"CodePink – and other organizations like it – essentially act like Trojan horses. They burst in onto the scene, and they're meant to disrupt and destroy from within," Balling told Fox News Digital.

"They're really interested in dividing America and, in doing so, weakening it," she continued, "and increasing the friction between Americans by convincing some Americans that the American idea, the American dream, the freedoms we enjoy, all that sort of thing, that they are lies and they're not worth fighting for, and that our enemies are our victims."
POWER COUPLE OF CHAOS: HOW A TYCOON AND ACTIVIST BUILT A 'REVOLUTIONARY BASE' AT THE HOUSE OF SINGHAM
Medea Benjamin (right) and Olivia DiNucci (center) of CodePink protest against the U.S. war in Iran. (Fox News Digital)

The confrontation comes as House lawmakers convene a hearing on Tuesday, titled "Trojan Horses: Covert Foreign Malign Influence Operations in America," to examine a broad question: how do American activists, nonprofit organizations, media operations and social media influencers, like Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, advance the interests of adversarial nations, including China, Iran and Cuba, inside the United States?
Piker joined CodePink's delegation to Cuba earlier this year, posing for a photo in Havana with CodePink cofounder, Jodie Evans, both of them also drawing Treasury Department scrutiny.

"Adversarial nations like China, Russia, and Cuba conduct malign influence operations here in the United States by utilizing social media influencers such as Hasan Piker as proxies to promote communism and push their false propaganda," Rep. Bill Huizenga, R-Mich., chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, told Fox News Digital.
"My goal is to raise the curtain to expose these operations and stop them from undermining our national security, capitalism and the American Dream," Huizenga said.
HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA

Democratic Socialists of America member Hasan Piker and CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans of CodePink meet in Cuba, as part of "United Front" to support the communist regime. (NO ACCESS EDGE/NNS/FNS/OUTKICK) (CodePink via Storyful)

The hearing will bring together several strands of alleged foreign influence that Fox News Digital has documented over the past year through investigations into money, political organizing, overseas travel, media operations and relationships between American activists and foreign entities and interests. Most of the groups fall into the "red-green alliance" of socialist and communist groups, symbolized by the color red, working closely with Islamist groups, such as the anti-Israel organization Students for Justice in Palestine, reflected by the color green, a symbol of Islam.

The largest financial network examined in Fox News Digital's reporting centers on Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon who lives in Shanghai, late last year standing on a stage at the Golden Tulip Hotel during a conference on the "Global South," delivering a speech supporting the Chinese Communist Party, China's leader, Xi Jinping and China's "new world order."
RUBIO'S CALL TO COMBAT GLOBAL FUNDERS OF FAR-LEFT TERRORISM COULD PUT SINGHAM IN CROSSHAIRS

A five-part Fox News Digital investigation published earlier this year examined 223 transactions totaling $591 million across five continents between 2017 and 2025, tracing the flow of money through multiple layers of organizations and into a transnational network estimated at approximately 2,000 organizations.

In 2017, Singham married Evans, the CodePink co-founder, in a ceremony in Jamaica attended by Benjamin and other pro-communist leaders. The Fox News Digital analysis documented $278 million flowing from Singham into six core nonprofit organizations that promulgate anti-America, pro-China propaganda, beginning in 2017: BreakThrough BT Media Inc., CodePink Women for Peace, Justice and Education Fund Inc., People's Forum Inc., People's Support Foundation Ltd. and Tricontinental Ltd.
The organizations and their executives have denied any wrongdoing and allege they are the target of anti-communist "witch hunts." Singham hasn't responded to repeated requests for comment.
CUBA BUILT COVERT NETWORK INSIDE AMERICA THROUGH SPIES, ACTIVISTS AND UNIVERSITIES, STATE DEPT ALLEGES

On Feb. 14, 2018, Jodie Evans, co-founder founder of CodePink, and Neville Roy Singham, founder of Thoughtworks, attend V20: The Red Party, a 20th anniversary celebration of V-Day and The Vagina Monologues, featuring a performance by playwright Eve Ensler and an after-party at Carnegie Hall in New York City. (Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images)

Huizenga and the hearing's witnesses say Congress must examine whether adversarial governments are influencing American political discourse through domestic messengers while keeping the foreign power itself at arm's length.
Fox News Digital's reporting followed the money to the six nonprofits:
$167.5 million to People's Support Foundation Ltd., a nonprofit based in Chicago, with CodePink's Evans on the board, funneling money to overseas projects;
$68.7 million to Justice and Education Fund Inc., a New York City-based nonprofit that funnels grants to far-left causes domestically and overseas;
$22.44 million to the People's Forum, a hub for pro-communist organizing in New York City;
$16.76 million to Tricontinental Ltd., a Massachusetts-based think tank led by a friend of Singham's, Vijay Prashad, who led a session on the future of Marxism at Singham's wedding to Evans.
$1.33 million to CodePink, a California-based far-left, pro-Cuba, pro-China group that has supported the Islamic Republic of Iran and anti-Israel campaigns;

$1.098 million to BreakThrough BT Media, a New York-based propaganda arm of the network that runs BreakThrough News, a media outfit that is often the first to broadcast images and videos of anti-America protests.

That was only the first layer. The six nonprofits that directly received Singham money subsequently distributed approximately $163 million to 52 organizations — including themselves — and five geographic regions identified in financial records.

Eleven groups at another layer distributed approximately $150 million into four nonprofits and five geographic regions, including $23 million directed to Sub-Saharan Africa, according to the Fox News Digital analysis.

The financial architecture has been accompanied by political organizing, media operations and ideological activity that includes the fresh example of political theater that CodePink unleashed at this week's disruption at the Institute of World Politics' panel on Cuba.
Balling, the former advisor to U.S. Special Operations Southern Command, used the opportunity to illustrate exactly the point that the Heritage Foundation's Gonzalez and she were arguing.
"Their method of operation," she said, "is to disrupt, of course, to get the soundbites on Twitter or Instagram or what have you, but they are not ever interested in a respectful dialogue."

"What was extraordinary is I was actually about to talk about CodePink and the Democratic Socialists of America, the DSA, as both being members of the largest pro-Cuban regime organization in the United States, called the National Network on Cuba," said Balling.

WASHINGTON DC, UNITED STATES - MARCH 6: United States Rep. Bill Huizenga speaks during a hearing before the House Financial Services Committee at the Rayburn House Office Building in Washington, D.C., on March 6, 2024. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"And so the fact that she stood up and tried to disrupt the event was just a wonderful example for the audience," of the antics of CodePink. "They are actually really a mouthpiece for anti-American causes, which happen to be very pro-Chinese Communist Party causes and...the Castro regime."

On cue, at 6:42 p.m., less than an hour after the event had ended at about 6 p.m., CodePink posted a carefully curated and captioned 1-minute-35-second video of the DiNucci outburst on X. The same video went up on CodePink's official YouTube channel.
Balling said CodePink's messaging promoted "the interests of, frankly, our enemies, the Chinese Communist Party and then the Cuban regime."

On June 4, 2024, CodePink's Medea Benjamin interrupts a Capitol Hill news conference in Washington, D.C., organized to commemorate the anniversary of the 1989 Tiananmen Square Massacre and to discuss the "ongoing struggle for human rights and democracy in China." By the end of the night, the disruption had also become a press release on CodePink's website, listing DiNucci herself as the "media contact" and offering journalists "unbranded video footage."

title: House Dems face Trump tariff dilemma as major Russia sanctions bill heads to floor
summary: The Lindsey Graham sanctions bill forces House Democrats to weigh Ukraine support against expanding Trump tariff authority they've long opposed.
story: A Senate-passed Russia sanctions bill faces resistance in the House as Democrats raise concerns about granting President Trump expanded tariff authority, while supporters argue tougher economic pressure could help force Moscow toward negotiations.

House Democrats will soon have to grapple with a decision over whether to give President Donald Trump more tariff authority or potentially block Congress from cracking down on Vladimir Putin's bloody war in Ukraine.
The House Rules Committee has teed up votes on several bills this week, including the Senate's legislation aimed at sanctioning Russia and Iran.
That bill was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a massive supporter of Ukraine who died unexpectedly at the age of 71 in July.

And while the majority of Democrats support action to help Ukraine against Russia's invasion, they'll also be forced to reckon with the legislation's language giving Trump additional authority to punish Russia and its allies with significant tariffs.
LINDSEY GRAHAM'S FINAL MISSION TO PUNISH PUTIN CLEARS SENATE AFTER YEARLONG FIGHT

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol building on March 27, 2026 in Washington, D.C. President of the United States Donald J. Trump during the 2026 Easter Egg Roll at the White House, Washington, D.C., on April 6, 2026. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images; Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Democrats have long been critical of Trump's unchecked use of tariffs against U.S. allies like Canada and Mexico, which have also been subject to a slew of court battles.
TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED
It's part of why senior House Democrats said earlier this year that they would oppose the bill.

"House Democrats are rock solid in our support for Ukraine, but the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia And Iran Act would do more harm than good. This bill would dramatically expand presidential tariff authorities while failing to mandate sanctions on Russia, both of which are unacceptable," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, Rep. Richard Neal, D-Mass., Ranking Member of the House Committee on Ways and Means, and Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., said in a statement.
SEN RAND PAUL: DC'S RUSSIA SANCTIONS BILL WON'T STOP PUTIN — BUT IT WILL HURT YOU

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., did not give up his position on the bill during a Monday press conference, telling reporters, "We're going to continue to stand by the Ukrainian people and find a path forward to get a sanctions bill done while addressing the very real concerns that [Democrats] have raised about giving Donald Trump authority that the Supreme Court recently made clear he does not currently have, and should not have, because it belongs to the Congress pursuant to the Constitution."
The bill would direct the president to hike up to 500% tariffs on Russia and up to 100% on countries buying Russian energy.
MIKE PENCE: CONGRESS MUST FINISH LINDSEY GRAHAM’S FIGHT AGAINST PUTIN
Trump would also be directed to impose significant sanctions on Russian officials and others responsible for continuing the war on Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, left, meets with Sen. Lindsey Graham in Kyiv, Ukraine, on March 18, 2024. (Ukrainian Presidency/Anadolu via Getty Images)
The bill advanced through the House Rules Committee on Monday night, setting up a House-wide procedural hurdle called a "rule vote" on Tuesday afternoon.
If passed, the full House will vote on the sanctions bill on Wednesday afternoon, according to a preliminary legislative schedule obtained by Fox News Digital.
And with an increasingly vocal isolationist wing permeating the House GOP Conference, at least some Democrats will be needed to help the bill pass.

The package, pushed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., and Graham, was in purgatory for nearly two years as the lawmakers and administration went back and forth to find a compromise that Trump and Congress could stomach.

Blumenthal defended the tariff language in the bill to Fox News Digital, "If Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously."
And Senate Democrats largely voted in favor of giving Trump limited tariff authority in exchange for the bone-crushing sanctions against Russia, despite raging against duties for years.

In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow on September 5, 2026. (Gavriil GRIGOROV / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
Though some raised concerns, like Sens. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., most Democratic caucus members gave a thumbs-up to the tariff power.
EXCLUSIVE: PENCE PUSHES TO RENAME BILL FOR LINDSEY GRAHAM, RECALLS FINAL TALK: 'BRING PUTIN TO THE TABLE'
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

That all came after Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., received guarantees from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the tariffs baked into the sanctions package would just be limited to the top five energy trading partners with the Kremlin.

title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to revive strict mail-ballot rules before midterms
summary: A lower court's nationwide block on U.S. Postal Service mail-in ballot rules remains after the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration.
story: Jason Snead accused Democratic-led states of resisting new USPS mail-ballot standards, while attorney Gregory Teufel argued the federal court overstepped its authority in blocking their implementation.

The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s emergency bid to enforce new U.S. Postal Service (USPS) restrictions on mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, leaving a lower court’s nationwide block in place.

In a brief order, the court said the government was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" for purposes of obtaining emergency relief and had not shown that the legal and practical considerations warranted a stay.
The rules would require federal ballot mail to be sent in envelopes bearing an election-mail logo, capable of being scanned by high-speed equipment and carrying a barcode unique to each voter.
State and local election officials would also be required to submit envelope designs to the Postal Service for review and upload basic voter information to an online USPS portal.
USPS PUBLISHES RULE TO BLOCK MAIL-IN BALLOTS FROM STATES THAT DON'T PROVIDE VOTER LISTS
A large box of pre-assembled mail-in ballots at the Wake County Board of Elections on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Raleigh, N.C. (Matt Ramey/AP Photo)
Under the USPS rule, mailings that failed to comply would not be accepted and would instead be returned to election officials to correct and resubmit.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION FROM RESTRICTING MAIL-IN BALLOTS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
A federal judge previously blocked the USPS from implementing the rules, including the online portal that could be used to track millions of mail ballots.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed with the Supreme Court’s decision but indicated the USPS may ultimately have the authority to impose the requirements.
TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS
Oregon residents drop off their ballots near the Multnomah County Elections building in Portland, Oregon, on Nov. 3, 2020. (Ankur Dholakia/AFP via Getty Images)

"In my view, based on the briefing the Court has received at this interim stage, there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority," Kavanaugh wrote.

However, he said attempting to apply the rules during the 2026 elections would be "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act because state and local election officials do not have enough time to reasonably implement them.
JACKSON RIPS INTO SUPREME COURT COLLEAGUES' 'SERIOUS LEGAL ERROR' ON TRUMP MAIL-IN VOTING ORDER

Supreme Court Associate Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas wait to leave the stage after the inauguration ceremonies in the Rotunda of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla/AFP via Getty Images)
Justice Samuel Alito dissented from the decision, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas.
Alito argued that some of the plaintiffs lacked legal standing and that the remaining challengers were pursuing what the court has previously called a "Hail Mary pass" that "rarely succeeds."
ALABAMA AG MARSHALL FIRES BACK AT USPS MAIL-BALLOT ORDER CRITICS: ‘THIS IS ABOUT SECURING ELECTIONS’
"The Government has made the showings necessary for a stay, so I respectfully dissent," Alito wrote.

Alito said the USPS has broad authority to regulate the collection, handling, transportation and delivery of mail. He also argued that the government would suffer irreparable harm because any reversal of the lower court’s injunction would come too late for the midterms.
New York Attorney General Letitia James, whose office helped lead the legal challenge, celebrated the decision as a victory for voters.

"Today, the Supreme Court protected one of our most fundamental, inalienable rights – the right to make your voice heard at the ballot box," James said. "This last-minute change could have thrown our elections into chaos, and I am truly relieved the Court granted this reprieve."

"Voters should never have to wonder whether a ballot they legally cast will be counted because the federal government suddenly changed the rules," she added. "We will keep fighting to make sure every eligible ballot is counted come November."
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., also praised the ruling, calling it "one of the most important cases to protect voting rights before the Supreme Court."
"Trump’s plan to make it harder to vote was obviously unconstitutional," Schumer said. "The Supreme Court had no choice but to make the right decision."
"The President’s attempt to screw around with vote by mail was obscene," he added. "Finally, his scheme is dead. Trump: you lost another one."
FEDERAL JUDGE AGAIN BLOCKS TRUMP'S MAIL BALLOT ORDER JUST BEFORE MIDTERMS
President Donald Trump directed the USPS earlier this year to develop new standards for handling election mail. The agency finalized the requirements in late August.
The administration and the USPS then asked the Supreme Court to intervene after a federal judge converted a temporary restraining order into a nationwide preliminary injunction.

The decision leaves the preliminary injunction in place, preventing the USPS from enforcing the new requirements for the 2026 elections while the litigation continues.
