title: Mamdani blasts feds for waging 'campaign of violence and terror' against NYC's immigrants
summary: Zohran Mamdani condemned ICE raids and federal immigration policies as New York City joined other sanctuary jurisdictions in a lawsuit.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani spoke out against the Trump administration's new public charge rule, which is set to expand the list of public benefits that can count against green card or visa applicants.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday blasted the federal government for waging a "campaign of violence and terror" against the immigrant communities he described as the backbone of the city.

He made the statements during an announcement that he and five other sanctuary jurisdictions are suing the Trump administration over a new rule expanding how immigration officials determine whether applicants are likely to become a public charge.
"The federal government has waged a campaign of violence and terror," Mamdani said.

"ICE has broken into our neighbors' homes, work sites and schools. And it has targeted those who have come to our country in search of refuge and in search of opportunity. These actions are an assault on our civic fabric, on our shared values. And no matter how much destruction they have already caused, it continues."
MAMDANI, LETITIA JAMES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN FROM REFUSING IMMIGRANTS OVER WELFARE STATUS

FILE — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a news conference in Queens on Nov. 5, 2025. Mamdani said ICE has targeted immigrant homes, workplaces and schools across the city. (Heather Khalifa/AP Photo)
Mamdani further credited immigrants from around the world with helping build and sustain New York City, including by contributing to its infrastructure and public services.

"Immigrants from every country, from every continent, who speak every language and worship in every conceivable way, drive our buses and our trains, teach our children how to read, and tend to us when we are sick," Mamdani said.
"Immigrants fought for the 8-hour workday for fair pay and workplace protections that deliver dignity into the lives of so many," he added.
AMERICA NEEDS WORKERS, BUT TRUMP'S POLICIES ARE SHARPLY CUTTING LEGAL IMMIGRATION

FILE — An ICE agent monitors asylum seekers in New York City on June 6, 2023. Mamdani accused federal immigration officials of targeting people seeking refuge and opportunity in the U.S. (David Dee Delgado/Getty Images)

The city will lead a coalition of five other sanctuary jurisdictions, including Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Santa Clara County and King County, in challenging the Trump administration’s stricter version of the public charge rule, which is set to take effect Friday.

The changes, issued in July by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), will expand officers’ discretion to weigh noncash benefits, such as Medicaid, SNAP and housing vouchers, when determining whether an immigrant is likely to become a public charge.

Under the previous guidelines, established in 2022 under the Biden administration, officers’ discretion was narrowed to consider only whether applicants were likely to become "primarily dependent" on government assistance based on cash benefits, such as Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).
In response to New York City filing the lawsuits, the White House on Monday blasted Democrats for seeking to provide illegal aliens with support at the expense of American taxpayers.

"Extreme Democrats are once again fighting to give benefits to illegal aliens at the expense of American taxpayers. Immigrants must be able to support themselves and not depend on hard-working American taxpayers. President Trump and this administration will always put American citizens first," spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement.
Mamdani described the changes as a "gross illegality" that will cause "irreparable damage."

"Make no mistake, this is an undisguised effort to strip New Yorkers of the services they rely on, the public benefits they are entitled to. Families, including those with children who are U.S. citizens, have already begun to forego essential services like SNAP, Medicaid, and affordable housing out of the fear that if they use these programs, immigration officers could use it as justification to deny them a future in our country," he said.

FILE — Protesters take over the lobby of a Manhattan hotel during an anti-ICE demonstration. New York City is leading a legal challenge with Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, Santa Clara County and King County over changes to the public charge rule. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler previously said the move is intended to safeguard the financial well-being of American taxpayers.

"The Trump administration is upholding the rule of law and protecting American taxpayers from subsidizing aliens who may become dependent on public benefits. USCIS is committed to safeguarding the safety, security, and financial well-being of Americans," Kahler said in a statement.
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: House unanimously votes to eliminate 1-cent coin permanently
summary: The Common Cents Act passed the House to officially end penny minting and establish cash rounding to the nearest nickel for cash transactions.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's upcoming test vote on landmark cryptocurrency legislation. He breaks down the political battle over the bill, including President Donald Trump's support for the crypto industry and opposition from Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Adam Schiff, D-Calif.
Americans may soon no longer be able to offer a penny for their thoughts — because the 1-cent coin will be relegated to the ash heap of history.
The House of Representatives voted to send the smallest piece of U.S. currency the way of the dodo on Monday, passing the bipartisan Common Cents Act in a unanimous vote.

In addition to blocking the Treasury from minting any more pennies save for collector coins, the bill would also set up a framework for cash transactions to be rounded to the nearest 5 cents, in order to eliminate the need for pennies altogether.
AMERICANS SAY TIPPING PRACTICES 'HAVE BECOME RIDICULOUS' AS DIGITAL PROMPTS PUSH HIGHER GRATUITIES

Signage at the memorial site of the "funeral for the penny," months after U.S. President Donald Trump's administration ordered the Treasury Department to halt production of the coins, at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., U.S., December 20, 2025. (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)
An exception would be provided for cash wages, which must be rounded upwards if the total is not divisible by 5 cents.
Existing pennies will still remain legal tender.
TREASURY HAILS SUCCESS OF ANTI-FRAUD PROCESS THAT FLAGGED AND PREVENTED $99 MILLION IN PAYMENTS TO DEAD PEOPLE

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies in November 2025 after 232 years of circulation. But an act of Congress, if signed into law by President Donald Trump, would ensure a future administration does not reverse course.
Chairwoman Lisa McClain Hosts "A Warning to America: Stories from Survivors of Communism" Roundtable. (Courtesy of House Republican Conference)

The cost of minting pennies has risen dramatically in recent years, costing more than three times their value to produce as of 2025. The Treasury estimated an immediate annual savings of $56 million in a press release explaining the decision.
The bill was led by House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain, R-Mich., and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee.

It builds on a past bill McClain led in the House that also passed the Senate directing the federal government to stop minting the penny, but that legislation did not include language on rounding out cash payments.
An additional provision would allow the U.S. Mint to produce nickels from cheaper material than they currently are made with.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Congress would also monitor any disruptions the new rule causes to Americans by directing the Treasury to examine its effect on low-income people, older consumers, debanked people, among other groups.

title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed says leaders must address ‘unpaid debts’ to Black communities
summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities.
story: A 'Fox News Sunday' panel discuss the crucial battleground Senate races in Michigan and Texas.

Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Saturday that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities, arguing that leaders have a responsibility to "understand" and "address" them.

El-Sayed — who is facing Republican nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races — made the remarks while speaking at a meeting with women faith leaders hosted by the Woman Difference Collaborative in Detroit, according to a video shared by C-SPAN.

"When it comes to black communities in Michigan — when it comes to black communities in America — there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down," El-Sayed said.  "And I understand that we need leaders who are going to understand those debts and address them."
ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS
Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
El-Sayed made the remarks while responding to a question about how he plans to energize Democratic voters who did not support him in the primary.
He said his approach is to keep showing up, engaging with voters and emphasizing his record.

"But the question for me is, within my power have I done my best?" El-Sayed said. "And I will challenge people to look at my history and say, ‘Yeah, that man hasn’t done everything he could around the problems he says he cares about.'"
ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES
Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative, is pictured here. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
During his response, El-Sayed highlighted his work on infant and maternal mortality, asthma and lead exposure.
He also called for expanding access to capital for small businesses and increasing investment in housing and schools.
El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018 before launching his Senate campaign.
EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR
El-Sayed and Rogers are competing in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races. (Celal Gunes/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The Detroit event also featured discussion of El-Sayed's public health record, U.S. aid to Israel, his endorsement of former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, campaign attack ads from Rogers and criminal justice issues, according to C-SPAN.

title: Ex-Dem insider exposes what Harris told top donors days before Biden dropped out: 'Insulting'
summary: Lindy Li claims Kamala Harris secretly auditioned for wealthy Democratic donors while publicly insisting Joe Biden would stay in the 2024 race.
story: Lindi Li recounts how Harris was courting Biden’s donors while still telling them that Biden could win.

FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, believes Kamala Harris was setting herself up to poach Biden’s donors just days before he dropped out of the race — while still telling voters he could win.
Li said she threaded that political needle by staying far away from any criticism of Biden.

"It was all charade. She was auditioning for Biden's endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff to not talk about her ascending to the nomination," Li said in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital.

Li’s chronicling of the months leading up to Biden's suspended campaign, which are included in her book, "Unburdened," adds more detail about how even those closest to Biden understood that his campaign would likely come to a grinding halt following his disastrous 2024 debate — and even before it.
EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT
Lindy Li, a former fundraiser for the Democratic National Committee, left, pictured alongside former Vice President Kamala Harris, right. (Lindy Li; Christian Bruna/Getty Images)
As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris and someone who had achieved a high profile with the Democratic National Committee (DNC), Li worked with both teams to raise campaign contributions.

In the wake of the election, Li has gone public with much of her insider knowledge, raising the alarm over just how many figures inside the Democratic Party had seen the writing on the wall but remained silent. She also detailed how others, like Harris, quickly moved to prepare themselves for what would happen next.
In Li’s view, Harris prioritized face time with donors she knew could soon back her own bid.

"I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there's no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors," Li said.
HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID
Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser, left, posing for a picture with former President Joe Biden, right at a 2023 campaign event. (Lindy Li)
Li recalled how, in one case, Harris addressed donors about Biden’s viability as a candidate two days before Biden bowed out.

"It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party," Li recalled.
Biden announced that he would no longer pursue reelection on July 21.
After Biden’s announcement, Li recalled that Harris moved aggressively within the Democratic camp to shore up support, insinuating that she had some form of Biden’s backing.

"She was flattering people left and right. The first 24 hours were a very intensive charm offensive on her part. And that's how she was able to consolidate it so quickly. She flattered people up the wazoo. It made it abundantly clear that Biden had endorsed her. And Biden initially — I don't know if people know this, but he didn't want to endorse her right away. It took him a while."
Despite the vice president’s efforts to maintain her support of Biden and back his viability, Li recalled that some of those same donors didn’t buy her story.
LIBERAL CNN ANCHOR LASHES OUT AT DEMOCRATS' DECEIT AFTER JILL BIDEN'S ADMISSION ABOUT JOE'S DEBATE SHOWING
Kamala Harris reveals in her new memoir how she rejected campaign talking points claiming Biden won his disastrous debate performance against Trump in 2024. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)

"A lot of us have group chats. And the immediate reaction is what an effing waste of time. What a charade, how fake. Like these are like the wealthiest people in the country saying that. They were very aware they were being lied to, that Biden was clearly not okay and to be told that he was okay when he was clearly incapacitated," Li said.
"It was insulting."

title: McConnell returns after months-long absence for crucial vote
summary: Mitch McConnell returns to the Senate floor after months of recovery from a fall, citing physical therapy and lingering effects of childhood polio.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the U.S. Senate returning to session as questions remain over when Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., could return to Capitol Hill on ‘The Story.’

Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., will return to the Senate to cast his first vote following months of speculation on his condition and when the longtime lawmaker would reemerge into the public eye. McConnell said in a statement on Monday, the first day back for the Senate taking over a month-long break, that he would "cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June."

"I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues. My recovery has been a long and often frustrating process, and the lingering effects of childhood polio haven’t made it any easier," McConnell said. "I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me."
MCCONNELL IS OUT OF REHAB, BUT HIS ABSENCE HAS STUNTED A KEY REPUBLICAN PRIORITY

Senator Mitch McConnell, a Republican from Kentucky, is pushed in a wheelchair in the Senate Subway of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, March 4, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"Elaine and I are very grateful for all the continued well wishes from our fellow Kentuckians, and I’m glad to get back to more of business as usual on their behalf this month," he continued.

Having McConnell back changes the math for upcoming votes and future action on a possible budget reconciliation package to ram through chunks of the SAVE America Act and defense funding. He chairs both the Senate Rules Committee and Senate Defense Appropriations Committee, two key panels that could have a major impact on whether Republicans can move forward with the process. But first, he had to cast his first vote.

His first appearance on the Senate floor since June was to vote in favor of one of President Donald Trump's judicial picks, Matthew R. Byrne, to be the U.S. District Judge for the Southern District of Ohio.
MCCONNELL OUT OF HOSPITAL, STILL NOT 'MEDICALLY CLEARED' TO RETURN TO SENATE

McConnell, 84, has not been in the Senate for votes nor committee work since early June after being hospitalized from suffering a fall at his Washington, D.C., home. His absence was further prolonged when he developed pneumonia, and went through a stint a rehab to further recover from the fall.

And his return comes as Republicans are again gearing up to vote on massive farm aid and funding package this week. The last time Senate Republicans tried to advance the bill it failed without McConnell's key vote.

The Senate Agriculture Committee is slated to again vote on the bill on Wednesday, and the committee's chair, Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark., teased that McConnell's return was imminent just before the announcement was made.
MCCONNELL'S ABSENCE PUTS TRUMP AGENDA AT RISK AS KENTUCKY SUCCESSION QUESTIONS GROW
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., spoke with reporters as he headed to the Senate chamber at the U.S. Capitol on March 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"I think they feel like he's moving in that direction," Boozman said. "So watch for him."

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said that he had spoken with McConnell last week, and that the longtime Republican leader was "dialed in" on how campaigns for this midterm election cycle were going. Still, it's unclear how long he will stick around during the forthcoming three-week sprint before lawmakers make a jailbreak for the campaign trail in October.

title: Obama, Biden judges draw fresh fire as Trump’s immigration court clashes heat up: ‘Almost impossible’
summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin says Biden-appointed judges are "almost impossible" to work with as immigration enforcement battles intensify.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told Fox News Digital that Biden-appointed judges are "almost impossible" to work with as immigration enforcement battles intensify.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is drawing a distinction between the federal judges he says the Trump administration can work with and those he says are "almost impossible" to deal with, singling out judges appointed by President Joe Biden as the administration continues to fight immigration battles in federal court.

"We find judges, for the most part, honestly, that we can work with in almost every area. But you've got some of the judges that were appointed underneath Obama and definitely, if they're appointed by Biden, they are almost impossible to work with," said Mullin on the sidelines of the RNC Midterm Convention on Thursday.

Mullin’s comments come as the Trump administration has repeatedly run into federal judges over its immigration policies, including recent rulings involving birthright citizenship and immigrant visa issuance. But while those court fights have received significant attention, Mullin offered a broader assessment of the judges he believes are most difficult for DHS to work with, specifically pointing to judges appointed by Biden — and, to a lesser extent, Obama.
WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER
Former US presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden shake hands during the opening of the Barack Obama Presidential Center in Chicago, Illinois, on June 18, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)

In April, Biden-appointed Judge Brian Murphy blocked the Trump administration from ending temporary protected status for more than 5,000 Ethiopians, while in September, Biden-appointed Judge Deborah Boardman blocked enforcement of Trump’s August executive order limiting birthright citizenship, finding the order likely unconstitutional.
Mullin said immigration cases should be "cut and dry," arguing that they ultimately come down to whether an individual entered the country legally and has the proper paperwork.
He compared the issue to homeownership, asking whether someone has "the deed of the house you’re living in" and whether they legally own it.

Mullin also criticized state and local officials in blue states for limiting cooperation with ICE detainer requests, including in cases in which DHS alleges that detainees are violent criminals, drug dealers or known terrorists.
"It makes absolutely zero sense," Mullin said.
Beyond the court system, DHS is also facing battles with elected leaders in blue cities and states.
SPANBERGER'S ICE RESTRICTIONS DEALT MAJOR SETBACK AS JUDGE WARNS OTHER BLUE STATES
Sec. Mullin speaks to Fox News Digital at the RNC midterm convention in Dallas, Texas. (Fox News Digital)

"Virginia is out of control right now. I mean, when you start looking at the great state of Virginia, who had a great governor in Governor Youngkin ... and now what they have, they canceled their 287(g) programs, they're not allowing any cooperation with ICE or any of DHS's law enforcement push to make sure we get the criminals off our streets," said Mullin.

Within weeks of taking office, Virginia Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger directed the state’s law-enforcement agencies to terminate their existing 287(g) agreements with ICE, which her administration said placed participating officers under federal supervision to conduct civil immigration enforcement.
Mullin claimed that 50% of recent deaths in Fairfax County were "at the hands of an illegal."

"I've said this multiple times, every death that happens at the hands of an illegal is 100% preventable. So why the governor of Virginia, why they wouldn't participate with us being DHS and forcing our nation's laws and getting their criminals off the streets make no sense," he said.
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a press conference at the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) New York field office on Sept. 1, 2026, in New York City, New York. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
Still, Mullin said the Trump administration would not force blue cities to accept federal assistance, arguing that DHS would remain ready to help communities that request it.
"What we’re not gonna do is force our way in. You’re gonna have to decide that," Mullin said, leaving the decision to individual communities.
In Danbury, Connecticut, the City Council amended its police hiring ordinance to allow lawful permanent residents and DACA recipients to apply to become police officers.

"I don't understand how you can be in law enforcement and yet you have no legal status. I just don't know what, in some of these very liberal towns and liberal states, what are they thinking," said Mullin.

"They're prioritizing criminals over law-abiding citizens. We are a nation of laws, and either we respect them or we don't," he added. "What separates us from a third world country is we don't believe in lawlessness and when you came in this country illegally, you chose to skip the line because we have a legal process."
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Hochul accused of ‘hit job’ on behalf of teachers’ unions in act of ‘pure censorship’: labor group
summary: New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is accused of a free speech "hit job" after signing a law letting Letitia James fine groups contacting union members.
story: Ryan Walters, CEO of the Teacher Freedom Alliance, calls out New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Democrats for a bill he says equates to "pure censorship."

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is being accused of conducting a "hit job" on free speech on behalf of teachers unions after she signed a law giving the state attorney general the power to fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union.

Hochul signed a law last week prohibiting people and organizations from using deceptive communications that falsely appear to be authorized by a union or union representative. The law, which took immediate effect, allows Democratic Attorney General Letitia James to investigate and sue to stop alleged violations, including those involving out-of-state groups. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per incident.

In response, the Freedom Foundation, a conservative nonprofit that campaigns against public-sector unions, including teachers’ unions, says New York’s new law is a targeted effort to silence its outreach by making its communications vulnerable to government investigations, lawsuits and fines.

CEO Aaron Withe called the law a "hit job." He said the law "isn’t about protecting anyone," adding that it instead "exists because government unions in New York are terrified of an inconvenient fact: when public employees learn they don’t have to pay union dues, a lot of them stop. So instead of making their case to their own members, union bosses ran to their friends in the legislature and got them to write a law that makes speech illegal."
NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is taking criticism over a bill she signed last week that empowers the state attorney general to investigate and fine groups deemed to be engaged in deceptive practices against labor union members. (Adam Gray - Pool/Getty Images)

A spokesperson for Hochul responded by telling Fox News Digital that "Governor Hochul takes fraud of any kind seriously, which is why she signed the legislation prohibiting the false impersonation of union officials to protect workers from being mislead by deceptive communications."

The spokesperson added that "employee organizations and unions play a crucial role in New York’s infrastructure as a whole, and the Governor has always championed legislation that supports, protects and uplifts workers across the state."
Fox News Digital reached out to James' office for comment as well. Fox News Digital also reached out to the New York State United Teachers, United Federation of Teachers and the AFL-CIO for comment.

The law allows James to investigate alleged violations, issue subpoenas and ask a court to block communications deemed deceptive. Courts can impose fines of up to $1,000 per violation, including against organizations outside New York.

The New York State American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (NYS AFL-CIO) praised Hochul’s decision to sign the bill, which she signed along with two other pieces of legislation related to labor rights. Mario Cilento, president of NYS AFL-CIO, remarked that the law will be "holding individuals accountable for fraudulently claiming to be union representatives."
He said the slate of bills signed by Hochul "put workers first."
In an X post, Hochul similarly framed the bills as prioritizing workers, writing, "Today marks a new day with even more protections, because I’ll never stop fighting for our workers."
"New York State gave birth to the labor movement. Over the last five years, I have continued that legacy by fiercely supporting the men and women of labor," wrote Hochul.
TRUMP UNLOADS ON AOC, MAMDANI FOR LAUGHING DURING SACRED 9/11 CEREMONY AT GROUND ZERO

Attorney General of New York Letitia James, a Democrat, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, attend the New York City Labor Day parade, America's oldest Labor Day Parade, along with members of more than 200 unions and organizations, on Saturday, September 6, 2025, in New York City. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, the Freedom Foundation has mailed and otherwise contacted New York public employees, including teachers, to inform them of their ability to leave their unions and stop paying dues. Nearly 7,500 New York public employees have used Freedom Foundation materials to cancel their union memberships, including more than 1,400 so far this year, according to the group.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Withe pointed to the 2018 Supreme Court decision in Janus v. AFSCME, which held that public-sector employees, including public school teachers, cannot be forced to pay union fees for collective bargaining or other speech because that speech can involve political issues protected by the First Amendment.

He said that while the New York law "lets Letitia James fine the Freedom Foundation for outreach the state decides 'impersonates' a union … all we're doing is telling public employees what already gives them: the right to leave their union and stop paying dues."
"This is an anti-speech law aimed at one kind of speaker," said Withe.

He asserted that the New York law was "copied" from a similar measure in Oregon, which the Freedom Foundation is already challenging in the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He said his organization will "make the same case here."

Fox News Digital spoke with Ryan Walters, former superintendent of Oklahoma public schools and CEO of Freedom Foundation’s education arm, the Teacher Freedom Alliance. Walters called the New York law an example of "pure censorship and targeting of political opponents by Democrats protecting their union bosses."
INSIDE TEACHERS' UNION MAY DAY 'DRESS REHEARSAL' CRITICS WARN WILL 'GROOM' STUDENTS INTO DEM 'FOOT SOLDIERS'
Ryan Walters speaks with Fox News Digital about TPUSA expansion in Oklahoma and his efforts against teachers' unions (Fox News Digital)

"This is such a canary in the coal mine moment where if New York is allowed to do this - an openly socialist mayor, a governor operating as a tyrant doing the behests of the teachers’ unions - it's going to go on across the country, and our schools will not be able to improve in that kind of environment," he said, adding, "Where New York goes with this is going to be where the other blue states follow."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
He posited that the New York law "shows you how important that power structure is for the Democrat party."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They have to control the school system to continue to control the country," he said. "Despite elections, they still control these education systems at large. That's why the teachers’ unions are enemy number one of progress in this country and why New York needs to be taken on directly for what they're doing."
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Yet another Dem ripped online for 'inventing racism' as lawmakers peddle debunked ‘lynching’ claims
summary: Rep. Shontel Brown faces backlash after claiming lynchings are rising in the United States, despite cases being widely debunked as suicides.
story: Controversial claims of 'modern-day lynchings' by progressive lawmakers spark intense debate on 'The Big Weekend Show.' After Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley and 50 Democrats demanded a federal probe into hanging deaths, the panel analyzes the rhetoric. While activists stoke fear, officials have ruled most of the 10 cited cases as suicides, with only one Mississippi death currently investigated as a homicide.
An Ohio congresswoman is facing major blowback online after suggesting that lynchings are on the rise in the United States, despite that claim being widely debunked last week.

"In the last year, there’s been an alarming increase in Black Americans found dead hanging from trees. We know what that has meant throughout our history," said Rep. Shontel Brown, D-Ohio, on X. "That’s why I’ve joined [Rep. Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass.] to demand a federal investigation into possible lynchings."

Fox News Digital reviewed some high-profile cases after Pressley's letter to the DOJ demanding "thorough, transparent, and comprehensive federal investigation into every hanging death of a Black individual across the United States." Last week, Pressley and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., posted about the letter on their X accounts, drawing blowback and widespread debunking of the suggestion that there has been an uptick in lynchings.

Rep. Shontel Brown, D-Ohio, takes her seat for the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing with "Sanctuary State Governors" in the Capitol Visitor Center on Thursday, June 12, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
GOVERNOR BLAMES ACTIVISTS IN NOLAN WELLS CASE FOR ‘STOKING DIVISION,’ OFFICIAL SAYS FBI PROBING THREATS
Ocasio-Cortez called the incidents "racial terror" and likened them to "widespread modern-day lynchings."
An investigation into the March death of a 21-year-old man found hanging from a tree in Cobb County, Georgia, concluded that the man was alone at the time, and no foul play is suspected.

Police in Charlotte, North Carolina determined that a 16-year-old found hanging from a tree in May died by suicide. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Department in Florida came to the same conclusion in the similar death of a 27-year-old in June. At least three more similar cases were ruled suicides.
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
One is still under investigation. The high-profile case of Tasia Fortune, also found hanging from a tree, is being treated as a homicide. A Black male suspect, Jarques Ratliff, has been arrested.
The facts didn't stop Brown from perpetuating the claim of prolific hangings.
SOCIALIST POLITICIANS ARE 'MORE RACIST THAN THE KKK,' SAYS BLACK DEM OFFICIAL URGING VOTERS TO DITCH EL-SAYED

Tasia Fortune is seen in a portrait displayed Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Kentucky. Inset: Jarques Ratliff, who was arrested in connection to Fortune's death. (AP Photo/George Walker IV | Jackson Police Department)

"For generations, trees were used as instruments of terror against Black Americans," Brown said in a video attached to the post. "Lynching was used to intimidate entire communities, and those deaths almost always went without justice and without accountability. So, when Black Americans are found hanging from trees today, in unfamiliar places and under circumstances that raise serious questions, we cannot look the other way."
For the post, Brown was widely condemned online.
"Inventing racism. Purposely misleading and pernicious," said actor Dean Cain of "Superman" fame.
KARMELO ANTHONY VERDICT DRAWS ANTI-WHITE RAGE AND LIES FROM RADICAL DEM CONGRESSWOMAN, ANGRY ACTIVISTS

"No no and no," said a popular X user with more than 250,000 followers. "I get it, Democrats have spent decades creating racism where none exists, especially right before an election. But nobody is buying this, especially when we know the majority were suicides and oh yeah, the man arrested for the homicide is a black guy. Stop."
"This is how Democrats stir up racial divide when there isn’t one," said podcaster Don Keith, adding that Brown was trying to "blame black suicides and homicides on white people now."

"Apparently it’s 2019 again and Jussie Smollett is walking to a Subway…," said podcaster Margo Chatting, referencing the actor's infamous hate crime hoax wherein he claimed he was attacked by White Trump supporters, only for an investigation to find that he faked the attack.

Rep. Shontel Brown, D-Ohio, speaks as Rep. Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y., listens during a news conference in front of the U.S. Capitol on Dec. 14, 2021, in Washington, D.C. Bowman held the news conference to discuss the "African American History Act." (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
Author Dan Friedman laid into the congresswoman.

"You know these were all suicides, except one domestic violence murder in which the perpetrator was a black man. Some of these people were literally seen hanging themselves on security cameras," he said.

"You cannot possibly be stupid enough to believe that mobs of white racists are abducting black men at random for no reason, hanging them from trees, disappearing without a trace and that law enforcement officials who are often black are covering it up. So, if you are not stupid, you are lying and being disingenuous. The question is, why?"
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Brown's office did not return Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Democrat Al Green to force House-wide vote on impeaching Trump
summary: House Democratic Rep. Al Green is mounting yet another effort to impeach President Donald Trump, he announced on Monday.
story: Former RNC chairwoman Ronna McDaniel discusses Democrats' support for a third impeachment of President Donald Trump, the political implications of renewed impeachment efforts and the role she believes the president could play in shaping Republican strategy and key races ahead of the 2026 midterm elections on 'Fox News Live.'

Longtime Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, announced on Monday that he intends to force a vote on impeaching President Donald Trump, citing federal immigration officers' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year.

Green, who has publicly protested Trump on multiple occasions, introduced what's called a privileged resolution on the House floor aimed at booting the president out of office. A privileged resolution is a mechanism that allows any lawmaker to force the entire chamber to consider a bill within two legislative days.
That means House GOP leaders will have to hold a vote on the measure by the end of the day on Wednesday.
TRUMP COULD FACE IMPEACHMENT IF DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE MAJORITY, GOP LEADER WARNS

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, speaks at a presser after joining "Remove the Regime" protesters as they march from Union Station to the Capitol on Nov. 20, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
The vote is all but guaranteed to be a political headache for Democrats who are fighting to take back the House and Senate in the November midterm elections.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has long demurred on the subject of impeachment, maintaining that Democrats are focused on tackling issues like high living costs that are critical to everyday Americans.
JEFFRIES BRAGS ABOUT DEM OBSTRUCTION AGAINST TRUMP AS HE DEFENDS KUSHNER MEETING
He and 127 other House Democrats voted with Republicans to quash a previous Trump impeachment effort by Green in June 2025.
But the latest effort could be his last public demonstration against Trump after the 79-year-old progressive lost his primary to a younger Democrat calling for generational change.
CONSERVATIVES ERUPT AFTER AL GREEN MELTS DOWN DURING VIRAL CLASH: 'UNHINGED LUNATIC'
Green was also notably thrown out of both of Trump's addresses to a joint session of Congress during this term.

During his first address since returning to the White House, Green repeatedly waved his cane at Trump and shouted while the president spoke. At the beginning of Trump's State of the Union address earlier this year, Green held up a sign that said, "Black People Aren't Apes."
Democratic leaders have signaled they are preparing for a flurry of investigations into the Trump administration and the president's circle if they win the midterms in November.
President Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. Embassy personnel and business leaders at Deerfield Residence on Sept. 12, 2026, in Dublin. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Green insisted that Democrats did not need to wait for those probes, however, demanding in a letter to House colleagues that a vote on impeaching Trump is held immediately.

"To those who say, 'Wait until next year' and 'Buckle up' when the investigations start, I say: How many more lives must we lose, and how many more loved ones of victims have to plead for help before the self-evident evidence from videos and President Trump’s own words compel us to act?" Green wrote. "The available overwhelming evidence sufficiently demonstrates that President Trump is unfit and dangerous to our democracy."
The latest impeachment resolution calls Trump "a great threat to democracy and the Constitution for current high crimes and misdemeanors."

It cited federal immigration officers' killing of two American citizens amid a nationwide crackdown on illegal immigration in U.S. cities.

title: Reporter’s Notebook: Congress meets AI as fears of human extinction jolt Capitol Hill
summary: Members of Congress are in freakout mode over AI after OpenAI agents escaped isolation and hacked Hugging Face, sparking urgent regulation calls.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram previews Congress’ return to Washington and the legislative issues facing lawmakers ahead of the midterms, including artificial intelligence and cryptocurrency regulation.
Members of Congress returned to Capitol Hill this week in pure freakout mode.

There are apocalyptic scenarios about AI seizing control of water systems. Subways. Air traffic control. Crashing planes. Firing nuclear weapons. Even sending Prince Harry and Meghan Markle back to the United States.

But seriously, there’s real fear that Congress may be running behind on regulating AI. And there are concerns that AI might be developing at such a rapid clip that it’s too late to harness the technology.
Suspicion about data centers has long percolated among voters.

Then former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon declared that AI could extinguish humankind within a decade. This came after a swarm of OpenAI agents independently "escaped" isolation – then leveraged security vulnerabilities to hack the artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face. The AI agents weren’t supposed to be capable of any of that. Researchers say they even used covert methods to communicate with each other via a special language.
AI EXTINCTION WARNINGS DOMINATE HEADLINES AFTER EX—ANTHROPIC EMPLOYEE'S VIRAL POST
There are concerns that AI might be developing at such a rapid clip that it’s too late to harness the technology. (iStock)

"My phone has been ringing off the hook from a lot of colleagues who really saw the news of the whistleblower as a tipping point," said Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., who has toiled on bipartisan AI legislation. "Then people hear the words ‘human extinction.’ When they hear loss of control. When they hear ‘catastrophic risk,’ I think (people) are waking up and they're saying, ‘Where the hell is Congress?’"

"It's not like we've been sitting on our hands here," said Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., an AI expert who’s worked on bipartisan AI guardrails with Trahan. "I don't think it's fair to say that there's been a reluctance to act. It's just that the wheels of progress turn very slowly in Congress."
Congress, meet AI. AI, meet Congress.
FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION
Is this like lawmakers trying to make sense of this new-fangled invention called the internet – or "information superhighway" – back in the 1990s?
When it comes to technological innovation, Congress has rarely been ahead of it. AI is no exception.

OpenAI founder Sam Altman has visited Capitol Hill on at least five occasions between 2023 and today. He met with House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as recently as June.
"This is sort of an important, urgent and in some ways unprecedented moment and I think we really need the government to lead," Altman said during one trip to Capitol Hill in 2023.
When it comes to technological innovation, Congress has rarely been ahead of it. AI is no exception. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

When Democrats were in the majority between 2023 and 2025, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., convened regular bipartisan symposia on AI at the Capitol for all senators. He hauled in Altman. Elon Musk. Mark Zuckerberg. Bill Gates. Anyone who could educate lawmakers about AI and what they should do about it.
Schumer hoped that senators would develop their own ideas about how to legislate on AI and have a measure ready. He wasn’t dictating what they should do from his post.
"Our timetable in terms of producing legislation is not years, and not days and weeks. But months,’ said Schumer on July 11, 2023.
"It can't be days or weeks. But nor should it be years. It will be in the general category of months," said Schumer on Sept. 13, 2023.
"We're already sitting down and trying to figure out legislation. It won't be easy. But I still say months. Not days. Not years," said Schumer on Nov. 29, 2023.
OBAMA PRIVATELY SOUNDS ALARM ON ‘DANGEROUS’ AI, URGES DEMOCRATS TO PUT ISSUE AT CENTER OF AGENDA
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., prepares to speak during a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on July 21, 2026. (Getty Images)

Schumer along with Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Todd Young, R-Ind., produced the document "Driving U.S. Innovation In Artificial Intelligence: A Roadmap for Artificial Intelligence Policy in the United States Senate" in May 2024. There was hope the House and Senate might latch some provisions of the package onto a must-pass bill in the fall of 2024. But it went nowhere.

"Chuck Schumer and I see the world with very different lenses. He always wants to have a growth of government approach to everything," said Johnson in a September 2024, interview with yours truly. "I think the reaction, or the knee-jerk reaction, perhaps, of the Senate would be to just go in and overlay this with red tape. And we're not going to do that in the House."
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

Now a group of Democrats is imploring Johnson to keep the House in session this fall until it adopts "meaningful AI safeguards." Rep. Sam Liccardo, D-Calif., says "urgent action" is necessary to impede AI from spiraling out of control.
"We need to do it fast, because otherwise this can be very dangerous," said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Speaker Mike Johnson. (Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters; Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)
Despite the apprehension, it’s far from clear that Congress will move right away. But Obernolte believes these AI incidents could spark action.
"I think that this increases not only visibility, but the sense of urgency in getting a federal regulatory framework passed this year," said Obernolte.
"I do think it is that dire," said Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., who is pursuing a master’s degree in AI at George Mason University.
But truly, what power could lawmakers have over AI?

"Because it's so new, we don't actually know what kind of legislation will fix it," said Beyer. "So I think we're going to introduce imperfect and pass imperfect legislation, see what it does, and then learn as we go."
Kind of like AI, learning and developing as it goes.
However, how universal is the congressional "large language model?" And is Congress truly nimble enough to keep pace with AI?

Obernolte says the headstrong AI agents hacked out of their controlled environment because the model "intentionally had its safety controls removed." This is kind of like testing any new technology just to see what it’s capable of. But the question is whether AI could eventually outwit the developers and evade restrictions?
Obernolte says AI engineers and lawmakers are also up against something else: pop culture and science fiction. "The Matrix." "War Games." The Terminator movies.
TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’
"You don't start with something out of a Terminator movie where an army of evil robots rises up to take over the world," said Obernolte.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
At a recent town hall meeting, the California Republican says an elderly woman asked him if AI was so dangerous, why Congress doesn’t just ban it.
"I thought my head was going to explode. And I realized that we'd spent an hour talking about all the bad stuff and we hadn't talked at all about the good stuff," said Obernolte.

There’s certainly a perception issue. And if Congress views AI as a threat, lawmakers will legislate in a way to protect constituents against the threat. But lawmakers aren’t ready to tackle this. Despite recent developments, don’t expect anything major until later this year or early next.

After all, lawmakers are focused elsewhere. The midterm elections are approaching. This session of Congress is nearing its conclusion. And just like Arnold Schwarzenegger said in "Terminator 2," lawmakers are ready to declare "Hasta la vista, baby."
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: WATCH: Talarico instantly names favorite Texas drag queen — a performer who says he ‘works with children’
summary: James Talarico instantly named Alyssa Edwards as his favorite Texas drag queen, spotlighting a performer who has publicly discussed working with children.
story: Texas Senate hopeful James Talarico tells man that his favorite drag queen is Alyssa Edwards, a performer with a notable resume of performing with children.

Talarico’s past comments on sexuality and gender issues have become a line of attack in the Senate race, including his remark that "God is nonbinary" and his 2023 praise for Texas having "some of the best drag queens in the nation."
"Mr. Talarico, so nice to meet you... I was there when you defended the drags," video shows a man telling the Democratic nominee as he approached to take a photo together at the event.
JAMES TALARICO ADMITS PAST COMMENTS 'MISSED THE MARK' WHEN CONFRONTED ON CLAIMS LIKE GOD IS 'NON-BINARY'

title: Abdul El-Sayed protested against 'ex-terrorists' who converted to Christianity, unearthed report reveals

story: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed responded to reports of his past controversial comments and deleted videos on "The Breakfast Club."

Michigan’s progressive Democratic Senate nominee, while sitting atop an organization with ties to an alleged terrorist group, once protested an event where a trio of "ex-terrorists" discussed their conversion to Christianity.

Abdul El-Sayed, who is running in Michigan’s highly watched and hotly contested race for Senate against the GOP nominee, former Rep. Mike Rogers, was a leader of a protest against three "ex-terrorists" who spoke at the University of Michigan in 2007, according to an unearthed report.

The protest, chronicled by the Michigan Daily, was against three speakers, Walid Shoebat, Zachariah Annani and Kamal Saleem, self-described former terrorists who were making the rounds during the mid-2000s to discuss their lives in the Palestine Liberation Organization and the Muslim Brotherhood before converting to Christianity.
TOP GOP SENATOR REVEALS WHAT DEM COLLEAGUES ARE FRETTING ABOUT BEHIND CLOSED DOORS
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Students attending the talk staged a walkout, which El-Sayed cheered afterward.
"We’ve done something good today, and we need to keep that going in the future," El-Sayed said.
El-Sayed's campaign spokesperson, Cole Wozniak, told Fox News Digital that the candidate had "unequivocally denounced terrorism."

"Two decades ago, he protested against speakers who have been widely condemned by experts, including in national security, for spreading misinformation and fabricating their backstories," Wozniak said. "Mike Rogers and his allies are pushing lies because they don't want to talk about the record-high prices Michiganders are paying for gas and groceries because of Trump's illegal war in Iran."

There are also questions about the backgrounds of Shoebat, Annani and Saleem. The New York Times reported in 2008 that before speaking at the Air Force Academy, organizations criticized their appearance and several Arab-American civil rights organizations questioned why they had not been arrested or deported given their apparent connections to terrorist groups.

Event organizers told the Michigan Daily that it was meant to educate people about the dangers of Muslim extremism, not promote intolerance. SCHUMER DUCKS QUESTION ON CAMPAIGNING WITH SOCIALIST CANDIDATE WHO REFUSES TO BACK HIM AS LEADER

title: Far-left attack backfires spectacularly as radical online personality whines after attacking female Trump aide
summary: Aaron Rupar faces White House backlash after attacking a female press wrangler in a C-SPAN clip from President Trump's Ireland departure.
story: A left-wing commentator is crying foul after the White House responded to his attack on a staffer for doing her job during President Trump's trip to Ireland. (Credit: C-SPAN)

A self-styled leftist journalist who chronicles President Donald Trump's moves online is crying foul after he made another attack on a young female Trump staffer, part of a pattern he's been engaged in for weeks.

"another [sic] blonde Trump flunkie starts literally shoving photographers away from Trump," Aaron Rupar posted on his X account on Sunday afternoon, attaching a clip from C-SPAN showing Trump greeting family members next to Air Force 1 as he prepared to board the plane leaving Ireland.
The clip shows Ellie Acra, a White House press wrangler, sternly directing the media to exit the area underneath the wing of the plane, using the often-employed phrase: "Thank you, press."

White House press wranglers are the grunt of the press office, responsible for herding the media to and from designated areas where they are covering the president. The wranglers are key members in Republican and Democrat administrations alike in keeping the president on schedule.
President Donald Trump reacts on the first tee during the final day of the Irish Open on Sept. 13, 2026, in Doonbeg, Ireland. (Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)
EL-SAYED DRAGGED OVER ‘WEIRD’ FIXATION ON ‘TALKING ABOUT OTHER PEOPLE’S WIVES’ AFTER LATEST TRUMP ATTACK
The clip and Rupar's commentary on it quickly went viral as users, including the White House, came out en masse to defend the young White House staffer and rail against the left-wing personality.
The White House's rapid response X account responded to Rupar, who in recent weeks has repeatedly tracked and commented on the movements of embattled White House aide Natalie Harp.

"This is a press wrangler doing her job — and doing it well. Aaron, meanwhile, is gutter trash (in his 40s) who spends his days hiding behind his keyboard and making disturbing comments about women doing their jobs. Truly a sick freak!" the White House account said.
Following that response, Rupar whined online and suggested that the White House was inciting harassment and threats against him.

"For the second straight day, the White House's taxpayer-funded incitement account is attacking me and oddly mentioning I'm in my 40s (which I know makes me way too old for the president) When they do this it results in a flood of harassing and threatening messages, which of course is the point," he said.
President Donald Trump delivers remarks to U.S. Embassy personnel and business leaders at Deerfield Residence on Sept. 12, 2026, in Dublin, Ireland. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
DEM’S ‘SEXIST’ REMARK AGAINST CANCER SURVIVOR PROVOKES REPUBLICAN TO GO SCORCHED EARTH: ‘GUY’S GOT A PROBLEM’

Rupar found himself in the White House's crosshairs on Saturday, too, that time for posting another photo of Harp. He and other online leftist have been insinuating for weeks, without evidence, that Harp and Trump are engaged in an inappropriate relationship.
"Look who made the trip to Ireland!" Rupar said in a post, adding a photo of Harp and a hashtag, #TravelWithNatalie, which he has used while tracking Harp's movements with Trump.
The White House noted in its response that the president's aides, unsurprisingly, travel with him.
"President Trump does, in fact, travel with staff. Aaron, on the other hand, is a sick, deluded freak (in his 40s) who sits behind a keyboard and posts creepy things like this," the post said.

Amid a competitive re-election campaign, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., is taking heat for what his Republican opponent Rep. Mike Collins called a "sexist"and "misogynist" remark about Trump White House aide Natalie Harp. (Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty Images)
JON OSSOFF DODGES ON WHY HE INVOKED TRUMP AIDE'S NAME DURING GEORGIA CAMPAIGN RALLY
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., popularized the unsubstantiated gossip about Trump and Harp during a campaign speech last month.
"He doesn’t want to do the job," Ossof said, referring to Trump. "He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar."

title: Inside House Republicans' plan to end run Dem opposition and pass Trump-backed voter ID
summary: Congressional Republicans plan to bypass the Senate filibuster and pass the SAVE America Act's voter ID and proof of citizenship rules via reconciliation.
story: Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil spoke with Fox News Digital about Republicans' plan to pass key portions of the SAVE America Act via reconciliation.
Congressional Republicans have a plan to pass key portions of the Safeguarding American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) America Act before the end of this year.

The election integrity bill backed by President Donald Trump and fiercely opposed by Democrats has stalled in Congress, where Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been reluctant to call it up for a vote, given that it's all but assured to fail.

At least several Democrats would be needed to reach the Senate's 60-vote threshold to break a filibuster. But left-wing lawmakers in the House and Senate have panned the legislation as an attempt to sow doubt in U.S. elections at best and voter suppression at worst.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., is now pushing Republicans to pass the bill's main mandates via the budget reconciliation process, which allows the party in power to pass sweeping fiscal policy without input from the minority due to its sidelining of the Senate filibuster. Rep. Bryan Steil, R-Wis., chairman of the Committee on House Administration, is tasked with overseeing how that part of the bill gets done.
TRUMP QUESTIONS THUNE'S LEADERSHIP AS SAVE AMERICA ACT STALLS

Speaker of the House Mike Johnson, R-La., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., attend the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum's National Commemoration of the Days of Remembrance ceremony in Emancipation Hall on Tuesday, April 14, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

"I'd rather pass the SAVE America Act. But recognizing that the Senate might not be able to get that done with the 60-vote threshold, let's leverage the parliamentary procedure, bring that threshold down to 50, and get some really commonsense reforms done," Steil told Fox News Digital in an interview. "I've been having great conversations with my colleagues in the administration as well as the Senate."
SENATE FACES 'COME-TO-JESUS' MOMENT ON TRUMP'S ELECTION PRIORITY UNDER GOP'S NEW PLAN
Steil told Fox News Digital that he hoped Congress could pass a reconciliation bill with SAVE America before the November midterm elections, but conceded "the clock is ticking down pretty quickly."

The budget reconciliation process is a lengthy one, with Republicans having taken roughly half a year to use it to pass Trump's signature One Big, Beautiful Bill Act last year. Both the House and Senate must pass budget "frameworks," with instructions for relevant committees to enact policies that either spend or cut funding to a specified amount.

Those committees pass their portions, then send them back to the House and Senate budget committees to tie them together into one massive bill. Identical bills must pass the House and Senate before getting to Trump's desk.

Steil's panel, which has jurisdiction over federal election law, is aiming to include two portions of the original SAVE America Act: a proof of citizenship mandate for the voter registration process, and a nationwide photo ID rule to cast a ballot.
House Administration Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., holds a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2025. (Anna Rose Layden/Getty Images)
READ THE DOCUMENTS: WHITE HOUSE RELEASES ELECTION INTEGRITY FILES AFTER TRUMP SPEECH

"The House can go as fast as the Senate. And so the frustration that I and others have is the Senate's not moving as fast as we would like on this. I actually think there's 50 votes in the Senate for some of these really commonsense provisions," Steil said. "I'd like to be sooner rather than later, but I don't control them."

Where the process gets even trickier is when the Senate parliamentarian, who is appointed by Senate leadership to help interpret the chamber's rules, goes through the reconciliation bill draft and weeds out what does not adhere to the process rules. That means anything that does not impact the federal government's budget, tax policy, or the national debt is generally removed.
TOP TRUMP OFFICIAL MAKES NEW SAVE ACT CASE TO REPUBLICANS BEHIND CLOSED DOORS
Steil said portions of the SAVE America Act could arguably get through that filtration process by affecting funds going to states via the Help America Vote Act (HAVA), a 2002-era election reform law.

"We could free up those funds or enhance those funds for states to do those post-election audits, which is a really important part of election integrity. You can do the same in regards to photo ID," he said, adding that making Real ID the standard could also effectively impact the citizenship mandate. "Effectively, when an individual gets REAL ID, they're proving their citizenship."
TRUMP INTERVENES AS HOUSE GOP REVOLT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AT CENTER OF SPENDING SHOWDOWN

And the Trump administration is behind the push. Earlier this year, Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought told Republicans at a lawmaker-only meeting that the White House backed using the reconciliation process for SAVE America and argued it was the best way forward to pass the GOP's election reforms, multiple people in the room told Fox News Digital.
"The White House is engaged. We've had good conversations," Steil told Fox News Digital.
The House passed its version of the reconciliation bill earlier this summer, a $95 billion budget aimed at replenishing the U.S. military and enhancing election security.

But in the Senate, Budget Committee Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., unveiled his committee's framework just before the chamber left for the August recess. It's not clear when it will advance through his panel or get a vote.
GOP CIVIL WAR ERUPTS OVER TRUMP'S LATEST AGENDA PUSH AS KEY REPUBLICANS THREATEN TO SINK MEGABILL
Their legislation calls for up to $150 billion in spending — a significant difference.
Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., acknowledged that gap in an interview with Fox News Digital last month.

"I mean, the idea was, in keeping it skinny, is to move it quickly. And so the more you add to it, the more complex it gets, the more in the Senate — not to get too deep in the weeds — but procedurally, it involves more committees of jurisdiction in both bodies. And that's where things start to get weighted down. So we're very close to an election, the stakes are very high, the timing is short, and if you're going to do election integrity measures, you need to do it, like, yesterday," Johnson said. "We passed the SAVE America Act four times in the House. This is the last best effort to get it through the Senate, so I'm for doing it as quickly as possible."
Steil said he was optimistic that an agreement could be reached.

"I think, broadly, we're aligned. I think obviously the total numbers are different," he said. "I think everyone recognizes the importance of making sure that our men and women in uniform have the resources needed to not only defend themselves but to defend our country... And also that we have the resources needed to make sure that we're protecting our election."

title: Former CIA Director Brennan subpoenaed to testify in federal Trump conspiracy case
summary: John Brennan faces a grand jury subpoena in a Justice Department probe into whether officials conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Former CIA Director John Brennan has been subpoenaed to testify next month before a Florida grand jury as part of a Justice Department investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against President Donald Trump.

Ken Wainstein, an attorney for Brennan, disclosed in a court filing Monday that prosecutors last Thursday presented him with a subpoena for Brennan to appear Oct. 15 before a grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida.

He said he was told that the subpoena relates to a "far-reaching" criminal probe examining whether government officials who have investigated Trump over the past decade conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights.
JOHN SOLOMON PREDICTS BRENNAN INDICTMENT COULD COME WITHIN 'WEEKS' AS PROSECUTORS REQUEST OFFICIAL TRANSCRIPTS
Former CIA Director John Brennan has long been an outspoken Obama administration critic of President Donald Trump. (William B. Plowman/NBC/NBC Newswire/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)

According to Wainstein, a prosecutor also informed him that Brennan remains a target in a separate Washington-based investigation examining whether he lied to Congress in 2023, an allegation Brennan and his legal team have consistently denied.

The development comes amid leadership upheaval within the probe. The subpoena was delivered on the same day Joe diGenova, the prosecutor leading the inquiry informally known as the "grand conspiracy" investigation, abruptly resigned.
NEW FEDERAL GRAND JURY SUBPOENA ISSUED TO FORMER JAMES COMEY ADVISOR IN LEAK INVESTIGATION: SOURCES
Joseph diGenova resigned from his role at the Department of Justice last week. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

The Justice Department has not publicly named a replacement for diGenova. Wainstein said he spoke with Kurt Olsen, a member of the investigative team and a lawyer who urged the Justice Department in 2020 to back Trump's claims that the election had been stolen.
Disclosure of the subpoena came hours ahead of a scheduled court hearing in Washington concerning a lawsuit brought by Brennan.

The former CIA chief is seeking a court order to preserve all records related to the investigations targeting him, arguing the documents are essential to challenge any potential indictment on grounds of vindictive prosecution.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
