title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO to talk AI — and gets put on speakerphone during industry summit
summary: “Data centers are great, and they make people wealthy,” the president told CEO Jensen Huang, whose company makes AI chips and hardware.
story: President Donald Trump on Monday called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an industry summit and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone.
Trump characterized concerns about AI safety as a “hoax,” while telling Huang in the middle of the All-In Summit that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development.

“The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax,” Trump said, suggesting that critics are “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen. That could be political people, that could also be China.”
Trump also lauded politically unpopular data centers, calling them “great” and saying they make people and states “wealthy.”
“It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years, it’s bigger than the internet and AI, you know, much more so,” he said, while adding that people “have to be a little careful” and do things “prudently.”

A video of Trump’s call, posted on X, was reposted by the Trump War Room account, which is associated with a Trump-aligned PAC. The call is also included in a podcast that Huang was recording at the time.
Nvidia said it had no comment on Huang’s exchange with Trump or whether they will be meeting soon to discuss these issues.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump’s comments to Nvidia, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of AI chips and hardware, come as AI leaders have called for slowing down development of the technology.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay over the weekend that AI development needed safeguards, which was quickly endorsed by Tesla CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, among others. It came after researchers at leading AI companies stepped down from their jobs last week and spoke out over safety concerns, some describing them as an existential threat to humanity.
Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats last week to prioritize the development of an AI agenda.
Trump, however, has firmly stood by his support for AI development. In a flurry of social media posts Monday, Trump described AI concerns as a “SICK conspiracy” and a “hoax.”
During the Nvidia phone call, Trump said he assumed Huang was on the same page as him regarding AI development; Huang said they were.
“We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people,” he told Trump during their call.

The Nvidia CEO, who helped persuade Trump last year to not send National Guard troops to San Francisco, sits on Trump’s council of science and technology advisers. He has lobbied lawmakers to allow sales of Nvidia around the world, which lawmakers have said could advantage China and undercut U.S. leadership in technology.

His conversation with Trump came as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who had been urged by House Democrats to end recess early so the lower chamber could take legislative action regarding AI safety, said this week that industry leaders should be the ones taking the lead on safety.

Johnson said Monday that Trump would call a meeting with AI leaders. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News that a meeting between Trump and the leaders was “in the works,” but no clear timing had been nailed down.

CORRECTION (Sept. 14, 2026, 10:39 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article and its headline misstated the event where Trump spoke by phone to Nvidia’s CEO. It was during the All-In Summit, not during an all-hands meeting at Nvidia.

title: Emmys 2026 red carpet and winners: Matthew Rhys, Jean Smart, and more
summary: On TV’s biggest night, the stars are coming out to shine.
story: On TV’s biggest night, the stars are coming out to shine.
The 78th annual Primetime Emmy Awards in Los Angeles’s Peacock Theater promises to be all about prestige TV, but on the red carpet, the stars are showing off their Monday best.

title: The 2026 Emmys air tonight. Here’s what to expect, how to watch and who’s hosting.
summary: Hollywood’s biggest night in television is back after a year of new beginnings. The 2026 Emmys will take place Monday, Sept. 14, at 8 p.m. ET.
story: The Primetime Emmy Awards, Hollywood’s biggest night in television, is back after a year of new beginnings and heartfelt endings.
Several shows in their first seasons have garnered multiple nods, with “Widow’s Bay” up for 19 awards, “Pluribus” 18, “DTF St. Louis” 13, “Spider-Noir” 11 and “The Beast in Me” nine.
Follow live coverage of the 2026 Emmys
“The Pitt” leads the overall pack with 25 nominations, followed closely by the final season of “Hacks,” with 24.
Fan-favorite “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” has nine nominations. CBS announced the end of the franchise last year, and the final episode aired in May.

Many other familiar shows are back this year, too, including “Beef,” with 16 nominations; “Shrinking,” with 10; “Slow Horses,” with nine; “The Bear,” with eight; “Abbott Elementary,” with seven; and “Only Murders in the Building,” with five.
Whether you plan to tune in live or track the winners online, here’s what to expect from this year’s Emmys.
When are the 2026 Emmy Awards?
The Emmys will take place starting at 8 p.m. ET Monday at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles.
Where can I watch or stream the Emmys?
Viewers can watch the broadcast on NBC or stream the event live online with a Peacock subscription.
Who is hosting the Emmys in 2026?
Add to Google
Add to Google
“Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” star Mariska Hargitay will host this year’s Emmys. Hargitay is coming off two wins this season for the documentary “My Mom Jayne.”

Hargitay follows 2025 host Nate Bargatze, who made a splash with charity donations for too-long speeches — a stunt with major returns for the Boys & Girls Clubs of America and mixed reviews from audiences for its execution.
When does the red carpet start?
E! will host red-carpet events throughout the night, with a preshow starting at 5 p.m. Live red-carpet coverage will kick off at 6 p.m. — but fans should expect a blue carpet, instead.
Which shows have the most Emmy nominations this year?
HBO’s “The Pitt” leads the nominations with 25, followed by “Hacks” with 24. Apple TV+ trails with 19 for the first season of “Widow’s Bay” and 18 for Season 1 of “Pluribus.”
Who is predicted to win in 2026?
This year’s Emmys pit longtime favorites against breakout stars, and shake-ups can be expected.
“The Pitt” is likely to take home a decent amount of hardware, and “Widow’s Bay” is poised to make a splash in its first year.

Jean Smart is looking for her fifth win in a row for the role of Deborah Vance in “Hacks,” another Emmys favorite. The win would be her eighth, tying her with Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman for most acting Emmys for a single performer.
Meanwhile, Rhea Seehorn is expected to win her first Emmy as the star of Vince Gilligan’s “Pluribus.”
“The Late Show with Stephen Colbert” is also expected to win. It won best talk series to raucous applause last year, just months after its fate was announced.
Longtime Emmys darling “The Bear” has already earned its first win for best guest actor in a comedy, which went posthumously to Rob Reiner.

title: EPA to repeal limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
summary: The move would overturn a 2024 Biden administration rule requiring power plants to control planet-warming pollution.
story: The Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday that it will roll back emissions limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants — one of the Trump administration’s most significant moves yet to undo the climate policies enacted under Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama.

The change would overturn a 2024 rule requiring power plants to use carbon sequestration equipment to control pollution; it was one of the biggest climate change rules implemented by the Biden administration’s EPA.

The agency also proposed eliminating all other greenhouse gas emissions rules, arguing that under the Clean Air Act, it doesn’t have the authority to regulate those emissions as they pertain to climate change.

In February, the EPA similarly repealed emissions rules for vehicles, which account for the most pollution in the U.S. today. The agency repealed greenhouse gas emissions standards for vehicles, as well as the legal conclusion that underpins its obligation to regulate such emissions in the first place, known as the endangerment finding. The moves announced Monday would essentially do the same thing for power plants, which are the second-biggest source of U.S. emissions.
If the newly announced rollbacks survive the expected legal challenges, they could prevent future administrations from requiring coal and gas power plants to limit planet-warming pollution.

“It’s part of a thematic effort to roll back air quality standards,” said Charles Driscoll, a professor of environmental systems and engineering at Syracuse University. “Trump has said he doesn’t believe in climate change, so he’s been working hard to try to roll back any sort of carbon control measures that have been implemented previously or might be implemented in the future.”
The announcement came during a meeting of energy ministers about “energy abundance” at the G20 summit in Houston.
The EPA said repealing the 2024 power-plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy.
“The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement.
Industry groups cheered the announcement.

“Overturning these examples of EPA overreach will help preserve and strengthen the U.S. coal fleet, protect grid reliability, and shield electricity consumers from higher costs at a time of surging demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing,” Michelle Bloodworth, a spokesperson for America’s Power, a trade organization for the country’s fleet of more than 400 coal-fired power plants, said in a statement.
Environmental groups have already sued the Trump administration to challenge its repeal of the endangerment finding. They promised to sue in response to the changes announced Monday, as well.

“This is full-throated climate denial,” said Patrick Drupp, the climate policy director at the Sierra Club. “It’s going to mean more pollution, more extreme weather, higher electricity bills because we’re going to continue to rely on fossil fuels. ... This is the administration doubling and tripling down on old fossil-fueled coal and gas.”
The Biden administration’s 2024 rule was designed to be phased in over time. It would have required power plants to sequester and store at least 90% of the carbon pollution they produced by 2032.

The administration said at the time that the requirement would benefit the climate and public health in ways that would far outweigh the implementation costs. The administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, the rule would be responsible for preventing 1,200 premature deaths, 360,000 cases of asthma symptoms and 47,000 lost workdays.
The Trump administration is reversing the policy when the consequences of climate change — intense heat waves and stronger storms, for example — are becoming more obvious.

Extreme heat has baked much of the world this summer. July was the hottest month on record in the U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and many locations set all-time records. Overall, the three months from June through August were the warmest ever recorded for the contiguous United States.

Last year was the third-hottest in modern history, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. The past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record, Copernicus data shows.
The litigation over the new EPA policy changes could take years and might not resolve before President Donald Trump leaves office.

“These cases proceed relatively slowly in the courts of appeals,” said Meghan Greenfield, a partner at the law firm Jenner & Block who oversaw the EPA’s Supreme Court docket for rulemaking during the Biden administration. “It’s not clear to me at this point that this repeal, the one that’s being finalized today, will be before the Supreme Court by the end of this administration.”

title: Gavin Newsom says he won’t run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
summary: The California governor said there was too much “crossover” between his base and Harris’, and that it would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else if they both ran.
story: California Gov. Gavin Newsom made a surprise announcement that he won’t launch a 2028 White House bid if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to run again.
“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom told CNN in an interview that aired Monday evening.
Newsom said running against Harris, a fellow California Democrat who was the state’s attorney general before she became a senator, would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else.

“They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn’t trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever,” said Newsom, who has been considering a White House run.
Newsom, who has not run for president before, acknowledged that an “approach to the campaign” would be to say Harris, who ran in 2020 and 2024, had had a shot and has previously run for president.
“That would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one, actually. You know, that’s objectively true,” Newsom said, adding that the Venn diagram between them had too much crossover.
“I know her base of supporters; I know her friends,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.”
Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Newsom’s remarks.
Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on his CNN remarks.
Harris has not said whether she will launch a bid for 2028. She said in July that she has “not made a decision” and that she is focused on the midterm elections.
Harris said this year that she was weighing making a third presidential run, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton at an April event that she was “thinking about it.”

Newsom, whose term as governor is up in a few months, had previously said he would decide whether to run after the midterms, telling CBS News last year that he would seriously consider the notion after the 2026 elections. He recently traveled to South Carolina — the first state to hold a Democratic primary in 2028 — and confirmed he was considering a presidential run.

title: Pentagon inspector general says Iran war has led to a shortfall of U.S. munitions
summary: It’s the first public report on the ongoing war started Feb. 28 by the U.S. and Israel.
story: WASHINGTON — The Defense Department’s inspector general released its first report on the war with Iran on Monday, saying the conflict has resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains as the Trump administration works to replenish weaponry.

“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied reports that the U.S. is running low on munitions.

President Donald Trump said Monday on Truth Social that the U.S. is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.”
Two weeks ago, Trump posted that the U.S. had “virtually unlimited” amounts of ammunition and lashed out at reports of munitions shortfalls.

The congressionally mandated report covers from the start of the war on Feb. 28 through June 30. It is one of the first public accountings from any government agency detailing the cost, scope and scale of the U.S.- and Israel-led conflict to the U.S. military, the State Department and other agencies. It follows reports of low morale among U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East, a depleting stockpile of key munitions and extensive damage to American military and intelligence assets in the region.
Among the findings, the report provides one of the first government confirmations that Iran targeted the U.S. Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, in Bahrain, with drones and ballistic missiles.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

It does not address what was most likely a U.S. strike on an elementary school in Iran during the initial hours of strikes. The military has yet to release an internal investigation into the bombing; NBC News reported in June that a report was being finalized.
The watchdog’s report details the damage to military equipment, aircraft and other materiel over the first four months of the war, including the destruction of at least 30 large U.S. drones.

It says the war with Iran has cost roughly $33.4 billion, which does not account for repairing damaged facilities. It does include $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion for equipment losses and $7.4 billion in other expenditures.

NBC News reported in July that the war had so far cost $80 billion to $100 billion, according to three U.S. officials and three people familiar with the internal cost estimates. The Pentagon publicly said in July that the war cost $37.5 billion. Its estimate does not include the cost of replacing aircraft, repairing U.S. bases and replenishing critical weaponry.
Trump initially said the war would last for only weeks. But over the weekend, he said it might not end until “right after” November’s midterm elections or perhaps before.
The report also finds that the war has displaced more than 20,000 U.S. military and diplomatic personnel, who were relocated at the outset of the conflict and in the days and weeks after.

Most medical evaluations of injured U.S. forces were carried out on the ground, some by local ambulances, and the patients were taken to local treatment facilities because airlift capabilities had been moved because of concerns.
And U.S. forces flew as many as 5,000 flights from European bases in support of the war, though Trump has bitterly complained that European allies have not done enough to help support the war.

The report catalogs some of the damage to U.S. aircraft and other military gear, as well as some of the American bases in the region. Aircraft costs, for example, include destruction or extensive damage to four F-15E jet fighters, an F-35A Joint Strike Fighter and an A-10 Warthog, which was also destroyed, according to the report. Twelve KC-135 refuelers and nine other aircraft were also destroyed, the report says. More than 30 MQ-9 drones had also been destroyed as of June, according to the report, citing the Congressional Research Service.

The State Department sustained more than $208 million in damage in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — according to the report. That includes $184 million in damages to “diplomatic facilities” and $25 million more due to delays in construction projects, the report says.

The damage Iran inflicted on U.S. military bases had been far more extensive than is publicly known, NBC News reported in April. Iran also caused more damage to America’s intelligence and surveillance assets in the region than U.S. spy agencies have ever endured, and it is estimated to cost billions to repair, NBC News reported last month.
The report does not touch on the morale of U.S. troops who have been deployed as part of the war effort.

In recent weeks, concerns about deteriorating conditions for troops serving in the Middle East on the USS Abraham Lincoln during an extended deployment had escalated, and the Pentagon announced it was replacing the aircraft carrier.
The Lincoln is en route back to its port in San Diego after a stop in Thailand.

title: Bob Mackie, legendary designer who dressed Cher and Diana Ross, dies at 87
summary: Legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, whose sequined gowns for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and other stars dazzled red carpets for decades, has sewn his final stitch.
story: Legendary fashion and costume designer Bob Mackie, whose sequined gowns for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and other stars dazzled red carpets for decades, has sewn his final stitch.
Mackie died Monday at 87, according to a post on his Instagram account.

“He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” the post read. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”
His longtime publicist Jenelle Hamilton confirmed that he died of pneumonia Monday morning in Palm Springs, California.

Known as the “sultan of sequins,” Mackie dressed some of Hollywood’s biggest names over more than 50 years. His creations for celebrities like Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli and Barbra Streisand stunned both performers and fans alike and remain some of the most iconic costumes ever worn.

“Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special,” Sir Elton John said on social media Monday. “His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood.”
“He loved glamour like I love glamour, but more than anything, we shared the same sense of humour and had so much fun together,” he added.

Born and raised in the San Gabriel Valley east of downtown Los Angeles, Mackie was a fan of movies early on. Dave Karger, a Palm Springs friend of Mackie’s, as well as a host for Turner Classic Movies, said Mackie recalled taking a cable car to downtown L.A. at age 5 to see Judy Garland in “Meet Me in St. Louis” in 1944.

“He, from the youngest of ages, was a true fan of great actors and actresses and singers and performers,” Karger said in an interview with NBC News on Monday. “So I think the fact that he then got to live his dream and be an important figure in that industry meant a lot to him.”

Mackie first attended nearby Pasadena City College before he transferred to what would become the California Institute of the Arts, according to his Television Academy biography. He dropped out to work as a costume sketch artist in 1961, which included sketching the skintight, beaded dress Marilyn Monroe wore in 1962 when she sang “Happy Birthday” to President John F. Kennedy.
Add to Google
Add to Google
A year later, he was hired by the man who would become his   lifelong romantic and creative partner, Ray Aghayan, to work on “The Judy Garland Show.”
The pair went on to win the first Emmy Award for costume design in 1967.
Aghayan died of kidney failure in 2011 at 83.

Mackie was briefly married to Marianne Nicholson, an actor known as Lulu Porter, according to her IMDb bio. Their son, Robert Gordon Mackie Jr., who worked as a makeup artist, died from complications related to AIDS in 1993.

His work with actor, singer and dancer Mitzi Gaynor in 1966 caught Burnett’s attention, according to a short biography on his website. Her producer hired him to design the complete wardrobe for “The Carol Burnett Show,” a post he held for 11 seasons.
A star was born.

Karger, who interviewed Mackie for a forthcoming book on Hollywood, said one of the designer’s most iconic costumes was made for a Burnett sketch lampooning “Gone With the Wind,” in which Scarlett O’Hara’s dress is fashioned from drapes and curtain rods, transforming her into Burnett’s Starlett O’Hara.
Karger said Mackie called it the “Wind Dress.” It’s now part of the collection at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.
He said Mackie didn’t enjoy attention but deserved recognition that came later in life.

“When you think of Bob Mackie, you think of his loud, vibrant designs,” Karger said. “You think of the clothes that he designed for Carol Burnett to wear on her show or for Cher to wear at the Oscars or in a music video. When you knew Bob Mackie, you quickly learned that wasn’t him at all. He dressed in a very conservative way, almost kind of, like, preppy with a lot of tweed.”
Mackie created bold looks for Streisand for the 1975 film “Funny Lady.” She posted a photo of a dress she wore for the movie on her Facebook page Monday.

“Bob Mackie was an incredible talent,” Streisand said in a statement that accompanied the photo. “He designed one gorgeous outfit after another for me in Funny Lady. He might continue designing creations for the angels.”
National Comedy Center Executive Director Journey Gunderson said Mackie found a potent communications channel in costumes.

“Throughout his extraordinary body of work, Bob Mackie understood the unique power of costume in comedy — to help create a character and become part of the creative energy that drove the comedy itself,” Gunderson said in a statement.
His work with Burnett, Cher, Joan Rivers, Bette Midler and Lucille Ball “helped shape some of comedy’s most memorable moments on television and stage,” he added.

In 1982, Mackie launched a ready-to-wear collection and a line of collectible Barbie dolls, which featured red carpet-ready dresses complete with headdresses, dramatic long trains and his signature sequined glow.

Throughout the decades, his designs took on an increasingly universal appeal despite — or perhaps because of — their sheer scale and luminosity. One of his most famous pieces, the flame dress, has been worn by pop icons Beyoncé and Turner, as well as Cher, with whom he also shared a lengthy creative partnership.

The dress, a version of which debuted in 1968 on “The Fred Astaire Show,” initially featured large gold paillettes. By the time Cher and Turner donned matching versions on “The Sonny & Cher Show,” the paillettes were replaced by smaller sparkly sequins that came to typify his work.

title: Bystanders chase down man accused of striking woman with stolen car on San Diego boardwalk
summary: The 25-year-old woman was hospitalized in critical condition, officials said.
story: A man behind the wheel of a suspected stolen Tesla drove onto the Pacific Beach boardwalk in San Diego and struck a woman before he hopped out and was chased by bystanders Monday afternoon.

The 25-year-old woman was struck by the electric vehicle around 12:40 p.m. at the intersection of Thomas and Reed avenues and was transported to a hospital in critical condition, according to the San Diego Fire-Rescue Department.

Around 12:20 p.m., San Diego Police Department officers responded to a report of a stolen Tesla that its owner was tracking. About 10 minutes later, officers located the Tesla driving south on Mission Boulevard. Officers attempted to stop the driver, but he did not stop and the chase began, police said.
During the pursuit, the driver struck a San Diego Gas and Electric transformer and continued toward the Pacific Beach boardwalk, SDPD said.
“Due to the increasing risk to public safety, a field supervisor terminated the pursuit,” it said.
The stolen Tesla then traveled onto the boardwalk northbound from Pacific Beach Drive, driving fast near pedestrians.

“I just heard some sounds down there, commotion like something hit something, and obviously he hit a gal over here. And so that was the sound that I heard,” witness Miguel Valle said. “Then a moment later I see a navy blue Tesla flying by me at least 50 mph, trying to get away from the pursuit.”
Another woman was walking on the boardwalk but jumped out of the way right as the driver sped by, surveillance video shows. She was evaluated by emergency responders, SDFD said.
“A lot of people dove out of the way very quickly, and it really could have been so much worse,” SDFD spokesperson Candace Hadley said.
“This is a very busy boardwalk. Having someone drive through this area is incredibly frightening,” Hadley added.
Multiple people witnessed the car driving onto the boardwalk. One beachgoer from Santee described walking on the boardwalk when the car came rushing by him.
“I was in the middle of the path and I launched myself off my bike,” Alex Srour said.
The man driving the Tesla stopped the vehicle in front of the Baja Beach Cafe, and Srour ran after him, recording the chase on his Meta sunglasses, which have a built-in camera.
His video shows a couple of other people chasing after the man as he runs into a nearby parking lot and falls to the ground. Srour appears to pin him to the ground, and a verbal exchange ensues.
In the video, Srour yells at the man to get on the ground, and the man appears to plead with Srour.
Srour, along with other pedestrians, detained the man until officers arrived and took him into custody, SDPD said.
SDPD is conducting a felony hit-and-run investigation into the incident. The driver was suspected of being under the influence, police said.
Lifeguards initially responded to the incident, quickly followed by SDFD and SDPD. A woman who jumped out of the way is all right, the fire department said.
Police blocked off the area of Thomas Avenue and Mission Boulevard near Open Bar for several hours following the incident. By 4 p.m., the boardwalk had reopened.

title: Donald Trump Jr. acknowledges Russian oligarch with ties to Putin hosted his lavish island wedding celebration
summary: The president’s eldest son and his wife, Bettina Trump, said Umar Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations” after their wedding.
story: Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Trump, acknowledged Monday that a Russian oligarch with ties to President Vladimir Putin paid for their lavish Caribbean island post-wedding celebration in May.

ProPublica reported that Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars in wedding-related expenses for the newlyweds and dozens of guests for festivities on a private island in the Bahamas that started a day after the ceremony. The festivities included a fireworks show, which ProPublica reported Kremlev also paid for.

“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” according to a post on Bettina Trump’s Instagram page, which was signed “Don & Bettina.”

It’s unclear why a member of the Trump family — who has made hundreds of millions of dollars during the first year of his father’s second term, some of it from cryptocurrency ventures that have involved foreign investments — would accept a gift from someone so closely aligned with Putin.
President Donald Trump, who did not attend the wedding or the celebration, told NBC News in a statement that it was “not a big deal.”

“I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day from the wedding. It was an ‘afterparty’ given in their honor. Not a big deal! I was not present at the party,” the statement said.

The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia of California, said on X that Kremlev, who has been sanctioned by the Ukrainian government, “spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”

On her Instagram page, Bettina Trump said the island vacation, which included other members of the Trump family, had “been planned well in advance as a fun weekend with friends. It was never intended to be our wedding weekend. When our original wedding plans changed, we simply decided to get married before it and arrived at an already planned weekend as newlyweds.”
She also insisted there was nothing untoward about Kremlev’s involvement.

“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” she wrote.

It’s not clear how long Kremlev, who is president of the International Boxing Association, and Trump Jr. have known each other. They both appeared at one of the organization’s events in Turkey last September.
“I am proud to call Umar not only a leader but a friend,” Trump Jr. said at the time.
Kremlev said that they were “joining forces” and that “together, we will protect the transparency of boxing and open the door for the next generation.” He did not elaborate on how they were uniting.
Representatives for Kremlev and Trump Jr. did not immediately respond to requests for comment for this article.

Kremlev became head of the IBA in 2020. The association’s website says Putin presented Kremlev with an Order of Friendship medal in late April for his “contribution to international sport and his commitment to the global boxing family.”
Shortly before the Trump wedding, Kremlev was part of the Russian delegation that went with Putin to Beijing for a discussion of the future of boxing in China, according to Chinese state media.
Trump Jr. has met with people with ties to Putin.

Then-special counsel Robert Mueller scrutinized him during his father’s first term over a meeting he had amid the 2016 presidential campaign with a person who he was told was the “crown prosecutor of Russia” and had dirt on Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton.

Trump Jr. responded to the offer in an email saying, “if it’s what you say I love it especially later in the summer.” The meeting with a Kremlin-linked lawyer and other Russians with ties to Putin took place at Trump Tower in June 2016 but did not yield any helpful information for the campaign, according to Mueller’s report.

While it is illegal for campaigns to accept help from foreign governments or from foreign nationals, Mueller declined to bring any charges in that part of the probe, because his investigators did not believe they could prove Trump Jr. acted “willfully” when he possibly violated campaign finance law.

Trump Jr.’s attorney, Alan Futerfas, said in 2019 in response to Mueller’s report that it confirmed that the meeting “was just what Don said it was, and nothing more, and that there was nothing improper about potentially listening to information.”

title: Supreme Court says Trump can’t enforce new mail-in ballot regulation
summary: The decision means a Postal Service measure that could lead to ballots not being sent to voters won’t be in effect for this November’s midterm elections.
story: WASHINGTON — Casting a decisive blow against President Donald Trump’s hopes of exercising federal control over the midterm elections, the Supreme Court on Monday prevented a U.S. Postal Service regulation concerning mail-in ballots from going into effect.

The court in a brief order rejected an emergency application the Trump administration filed seeking to block a lower court ruling that said the regulation was most likely unlawful. The court appeared to be divided 7-2, with two conservative justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, dissenting.
The measure would have imposed requirements on states for sending out mail-in ballots to voters. Typically, the Postal Service has no such role.

Implementing those significant changes just weeks before the election would most likely have caused major problems, and advocates feared it would make it harder for millions of Americans to cast their ballots.

Time was already running out for the rule to be implemented, with North Carolina sending out ballots Sept. 4 and other states following suit. There were also questions about whether the Postal Service even had the technical means to put it into effect.

Challengers, including various states led by California and nonprofit advocacy groups headed by the League of Women Voters, said the rule would cause unnecessary disruption ahead of the election and prevent people from voting.

“Today’s decision is a victory for our democracy and a powerful affirmation of the rule of law,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, said in a statement. “The stakes in this litigation could not have been higher.”
In a separate statement, Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, called the regulation “an extraordinary attempt to interfere with voting in all 50 states.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday night.
Trump frequently rails against the widespread use of mail-in ballots as part of his broader complaints, offered without evidence, that the election system is rife with fraud.

Under the new rule, states would have to submit lists of eligible voters to the Postal Service, which would then verify that ballots were being sent to people on that list before it delivered them. States would also have to comply with directions about envelope design.

Trump’s initial order envisioned the federal government’s creating and sending the Postal Service lists of citizens and forcing it to send ballots to those people, but the final Postal Service proposal did not include that provision.

In a dissenting opinion, Alito said the federal government had the better of the argument. Concerns raised by states about the difficulties of implementing the rule gave him pause, he added, “but it is not enough to convince me.”
Alito also complained that courts, including the Supreme Court itself, were partly to blame for the case’s being decided so close to the election, saying they had taken too long to decide it.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, another member of the court’s conservative majority, wrote a brief concurring opinion saying there is a “fair prospect” the Postal Service has the authority to issue the rule but added it had to be blocked because it was issued so close to the election.
The Postal Service issued the regulation at the direction of the White House, with Trump issuing an executive order about the issue in March.
Massachusetts-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani blocked the regulation, saying the Postal Service had no authority to issue it.

She warned of the risk of “significant disenfranchisement” if the regulation were in effect and noted that the Trump administration had failed to offer any evidence that it was required to combat election fraud.

Various states have said they would not be able to comply with the regulation even if it were in effect, although some have indicated they could. A whistleblower complaint last week said the Postal Service system for checking ballots was flawed and that it could cause significant disruptions if it were implemented.

Talwani said that while litigation continues, states can voluntarily comply with the Postal Service regulation but have no obligation to do so. She also said the Postal Service cannot refuse to send ballots.

The federal government has downplayed the impact of the regulation, saying in court papers that it is a “modest design and information requirements for ballot-mail envelopes.” When states send out ballots, the Postal Service would check to see that the envelopes were in compliance, and if they were not, they would be returned to election officials, Trump administration lawyers said.

Trump issued his executive order after he failed to persuade the Republican-controlled Congress to pass his SAVE America Act legislation, which would impose new voting restrictions nationwide, including proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter ID.
Talwani had earlier blocked key provisions of the executive order itself, but in an Aug. 24 ruling, the Supreme Court ruled she had acted prematurely.

title: Gavin Newsom says he won’t run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
summary: The California governor said there was too much “crossover” between his base and Harris’, and that it would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else if they both ran.
story: California Gov. Gavin Newsom made a surprise announcement that he won’t launch a 2028 White House bid if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to run again.
“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom told CNN in an interview that aired Monday evening.
Newsom said running against Harris, a fellow California Democrat who was the state’s attorney general before she became a senator, would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else.

“They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn’t trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever,” said Newsom, who has been considering a White House run.
Newsom, who has not run for president before, acknowledged that an “approach to the campaign” would be to say Harris, who ran in 2020 and 2024, had had a shot and has previously run for president.
“That would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one, actually. You know, that’s objectively true,” Newsom said, adding that the Venn diagram between them had too much crossover.
“I know her base of supporters; I know her friends,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.”
Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Newsom’s remarks.
Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on his CNN remarks.
Harris has not said whether she will launch a bid for 2028. She said in July that she has “not made a decision” and that she is focused on the midterm elections.
Harris said this year that she was weighing making a third presidential run, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton at an April event that she was “thinking about it.”

Newsom, whose term as governor is up in a few months, had previously said he would decide whether to run after the midterms, telling CBS News last year that he would seriously consider the notion after the 2026 elections. He recently traveled to South Carolina — the first state to hold a Democratic primary in 2028 — and confirmed he was considering a presidential run.

title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO to talk AI — and gets put on speakerphone during industry summit
summary: “Data centers are great, and they make people wealthy,” the president told CEO Jensen Huang, whose company makes AI chips and hardware.
story: President Donald Trump on Monday called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an industry summit and gave another full-throated defense of artificial intelligence after Huang put the call on speakerphone.
Trump characterized concerns about AI safety as a “hoax,” while telling Huang in the middle of the All-In Summit that the U.S. had to beat China in AI innovation and development.

“The robots will not be taking over. The AI will not be taking over the rest of the world. The whole thing is a hoax,” Trump said, suggesting that critics are “just playing right into the hands of a lot of people that don’t want to see it happen. That could be political people, that could also be China.”
Trump also lauded politically unpopular data centers, calling them “great” and saying they make people and states “wealthy.”
“It’s the oil of the next 20, 25 years, it’s bigger than the internet and AI, you know, much more so,” he said, while adding that people “have to be a little careful” and do things “prudently.”

A video of Trump’s call, posted on X, was reposted by the Trump War Room account, which is associated with a Trump-aligned PAC. The call is also included in a podcast that Huang was recording at the time.
Nvidia said it had no comment on Huang’s exchange with Trump or whether they will be meeting soon to discuss these issues.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump’s comments to Nvidia, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers of AI chips and hardware, come as AI leaders have called for slowing down development of the technology.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay over the weekend that AI development needed safeguards, which was quickly endorsed by Tesla CEO Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, among others. It came after researchers at leading AI companies stepped down from their jobs last week and spoke out over safety concerns, some describing them as an existential threat to humanity.
Former President Barack Obama urged Democrats last week to prioritize the development of an AI agenda.
Trump, however, has firmly stood by his support for AI development. In a flurry of social media posts Monday, Trump described AI concerns as a “SICK conspiracy” and a “hoax.”
During the Nvidia phone call, Trump said he assumed Huang was on the same page as him regarding AI development; Huang said they were.
“We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race in America. Every industry, every company, every state, every people,” he told Trump during their call.

The Nvidia CEO, who helped persuade Trump last year to not send National Guard troops to San Francisco, sits on Trump’s council of science and technology advisers. He has lobbied lawmakers to allow sales of Nvidia around the world, which lawmakers have said could advantage China and undercut U.S. leadership in technology.

His conversation with Trump came as House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who had been urged by House Democrats to end recess early so the lower chamber could take legislative action regarding AI safety, said this week that industry leaders should be the ones taking the lead on safety.

Johnson said Monday that Trump would call a meeting with AI leaders. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News that a meeting between Trump and the leaders was “in the works,” but no clear timing had been nailed down.

CORRECTION (Sept. 14, 2026, 10:39 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article and its headline misstated the event where Trump spoke by phone to Nvidia’s CEO. It was during the All-In Summit, not during an all-hands meeting at Nvidia.

title: Trump loyalist subpoenaed John Brennan before resignation last week
summary: The former CIA director’s team is trying to persuade a federal judge in D.C. to force the Justice Department to preserve records it may use to make vindictive prosecution accusations.
story: A Trump loyalist heading a “grand conspiracy” investigation into some of President Donald Trump’s grievances signed a subpoena seeking testimony from former CIA Director John Brennan just before he resigned from the Justice Department last week, his lawyer told a court Monday.

On Wednesday, Joe diGenova signed the document aimed at Brennan for testimony before a federal grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, Brennan attorney Ken Wainstein wrote in a declaration. After Wainstein reached out to diGenova after he accepted the subpoena Thursday, diGenova wrote that he would “arrange counsel” to speak with them. Brennan’s testimony was preliminarily set for Oct. 15.

DiGenova resigned later Thursday. On Friday, Wainstein said, 2020 election denier Kurt Olsen — now part of the prosecutorial team in the Southern District of Florida — told Brennan’s team that there were multiple “viable” grand jury investigations into his client, “including a ‘far-reaching’ investigation in Fort Pierce that includes ‘issues at Mar-a-Lago and beyond’ into whether President Donald Trump had his civil rights violated.” Another investigation is running out of Washington, D.C., looking into Brennan’s statements before Congress, Olsen confirmed.

“Mr. Olsen explained that Director Brennan was a ‘target’ of the narrower investigation, and the investigation for which he was now being subpoenaed was the ‘more wide-ranging conspiracy,’ as to which our client was a ‘subject.’ However, he explained that the narrower investigation was ‘still viable,’ and that the issues in the narrower investigation might also be part of the larger investigation, such as being overt acts,” Wainstein wrote.

Wainstein and co-counsel Daniel Gelber appeared in court Monday before U.S. District Judge Jia M. Cobb in Washington to urge Cobb to order the Justice Department to preserve communications about the Brennan case.

Brennan’s team, citing reports of the Trump administration’s widespread use of Signal to conduct official government business, is seeking an injunction to force the government to preserve communications for a potential future argument that the case is a vindictive prosecution driven by Trump.

“Director Brennan seeks nothing more than to ensure that the government does what it is already obliged to do — preserve all records and communications relevant to the government’s preordained decision to investigate and prosecute him,” his team wrote in a filing last month.
“The government is not going to disclose what it’s destroying,” Wainstein said in court Monday. “There’s a lot of really underhanded stuff going on in this investigation.”

Wainstein also said that the Justice Department had been playing “games” with the case and that it was engaging in a “pretty unprecedented example of judge shopping” by running the federal grand jury probe from the courthouse in Fort Pierce in the Southern District of Florida, where Trump-friendly U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon is the sole judge.
Public officials are operating lawfully and honestly in discharging their official duties, and they’re not entitled to regular rules, Wainstein argued.
“If anything, it’s a presumption of irregularity,” he said.

Wainstein argued that diGenova was the “strongest champion” of a case against Brennan — noting that diGenova called Brennan a “traitor” a few years ago — and that his departure sent “a very clear message” about the case. DiGenova didn’t answer a phone call Monday.

Jeremy Newman, an attorney with the Justice Department, argued that the Justice Department conceded that it had a legal obligation to maintain some communications under the Federal Records Act but that Brennan was making an argument that his constitutional rights were violated and that he lacked standing to bring the suit given that he hadn’t been charged. If he were charged, Newman said, he could take those issues up with a judge and seek remedies.

Brennan’s team argued that will be too late, because any Signal messages exchanged about the case will have long disappeared. Wainstein suggested Justice Department leaders were using disappearing messages because they don’t want “history to know about what they were saying to one another” about what he called a politically driven investigation.
NBC News reported in May that the FBI was interviewing current and former CIA officers as part of the investigation.

DiGenova told NBC News on Friday that a specific event sparked his departure but wouldn’t go into details about the matter. “Everybody was in their lane, and then some lanes got crossed, and then I decided to leave,” he said.

After diGenova’s departure, the investigation is being run by the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Jason Reding Quiñones, with support from Main Justice, according to a person familiar with the matter.

title: Emmys 2026 red carpet and winners: Matthew Rhys, Jean Smart, and more
summary: On TV’s biggest night, the stars are coming out to shine.
story: On TV’s biggest night, the stars are coming out to shine.
The 78th annual Primetime Emmy Awards in Los Angeles’s Peacock Theater promises to be all about prestige TV, but on the red carpet, the stars are showing off their Monday best.

title: Mitch McConnell returns to the Senate after three-month absence
summary: The Kentucky Republican was hospitalized in June after a fall. “Time to get back to work to finish the job for this Congress,” he told reporters Monday.
story: Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., returned to the Senate on Monday and cast his vote after a more than three-month absence.

“Today, I’ll cast my first Senate vote since I took a bad fall back in June. I’m really looking forward to being back on the Senate floor and seeing my colleagues,” McConnell wrote in a statement Monday.
He later voted to advance the nomination of Matthew Byrne to be a U.S. district judge for the Southern District of Ohio.
McConnell said his recovery had been “a long and frustrating process,” adding that it had been complicated by “lingering effects of childhood polio.”

“I’m still not quite back to 100%, but I’ve assured Leader Thune that, as I continue with physical therapy on the advice of my doctors, I will do my best to be present for tough votes when our Conference needs me,” McConnell said in his statement.
McConnell has been missing from the Senate since mid-June, when he fell at home and was “briefly unconscious,” according to a statement in July.

“I must admit, after two years, two decades after dodging your questions, I wasn’t sure how many of you would be here today,” McConnell joked to reporters as he sat in a wheelchair Monday. “So I’m glad to see you. Time to get back to work to finish the job for this Congress. I’m here to work on the farm bill.”
McConnell, who appeared frail but jovial, did not take questions from reporters.
McConnell was hospitalized after his fall and later released to rehabilitation care.

At the time, his office released a photo of him in a hospital chair alongside his wife, Elaine Chao. His absence, along with a lack of interview appearances in the media, led to rampant speculation and calls from members of the public and Kentucky’s Democratic governor to release proof that he was fit to serve in Congress or otherwise resign.
McConnell, 84, addressed why it took him so long to disclose the reason for his absence in July, saying he couldn’t help but hesitate “to share the vulnerability that comes with getting older.”

A farm bill is set for a markup Wednesday in the Senate Agriculture Committee. Republicans hold a slim 12-11 majority in the committee, meaning McConnell’s presence is needed to send bills to the full Senate floor on party-line votes.

McConnell, who is retiring at the end of the year, has faced several health issues in the past few years. He took a fall at a Senate Leadership Fund dinner in 2023, leading to a hospitalization and a diagnosis of a concussion and a rib fracture. Later that year, McConnell froze midsentence while he was addressing reporters on the Hill on more than one occasion.
McConnell was elected to the Senate in 1984. Rep. Andy Barr, R-Ky., is the Republican nominee for his seat in the ruby-red state.

title: EPA to repeal limits on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants
summary: The move would overturn a 2024 Biden administration rule requiring power plants to control planet-warming pollution.
story: The Environmental Protection Agency announced Monday that it will roll back emissions limits on coal- and gas-fired power plants — one of the Trump administration’s most significant moves yet to undo the climate policies enacted under Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama.

The change would overturn a 2024 rule requiring power plants to use carbon sequestration equipment to control pollution; it was one of the biggest climate change rules implemented by the Biden administration’s EPA.

The agency also proposed eliminating all other greenhouse gas emissions rules, arguing that under the Clean Air Act, it doesn’t have the authority to regulate those emissions as they pertain to climate change.

In February, the EPA similarly repealed emissions rules for vehicles, which account for the most pollution in the U.S. today. The agency repealed greenhouse gas emissions standards for vehicles, as well as the legal conclusion that underpins its obligation to regulate such emissions in the first place, known as the endangerment finding. The moves announced Monday would essentially do the same thing for power plants, which are the second-biggest source of U.S. emissions.
If the newly announced rollbacks survive the expected legal challenges, they could prevent future administrations from requiring coal and gas power plants to limit planet-warming pollution.

“It’s part of a thematic effort to roll back air quality standards,” said Charles Driscoll, a professor of environmental systems and engineering at Syracuse University. “Trump has said he doesn’t believe in climate change, so he’s been working hard to try to roll back any sort of carbon control measures that have been implemented previously or might be implemented in the future.”
The announcement came during a meeting of energy ministers about “energy abundance” at the G20 summit in Houston.
The EPA said repealing the 2024 power-plant rule would save industry more than $300 billion in costs and help “unleash” American energy.
“The Trump administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a statement.
Industry groups cheered the announcement.

“Overturning these examples of EPA overreach will help preserve and strengthen the U.S. coal fleet, protect grid reliability, and shield electricity consumers from higher costs at a time of surging demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, and advanced manufacturing,” Michelle Bloodworth, a spokesperson for America’s Power, a trade organization for the country’s fleet of more than 400 coal-fired power plants, said in a statement.
Environmental groups have already sued the Trump administration to challenge its repeal of the endangerment finding. They promised to sue in response to the changes announced Monday, as well.

“This is full-throated climate denial,” said Patrick Drupp, the climate policy director at the Sierra Club. “It’s going to mean more pollution, more extreme weather, higher electricity bills because we’re going to continue to rely on fossil fuels. ... This is the administration doubling and tripling down on old fossil-fueled coal and gas.”
The Biden administration’s 2024 rule was designed to be phased in over time. It would have required power plants to sequester and store at least 90% of the carbon pollution they produced by 2032.

The administration said at the time that the requirement would benefit the climate and public health in ways that would far outweigh the implementation costs. The administration estimated that in the year 2035 alone, the rule would be responsible for preventing 1,200 premature deaths, 360,000 cases of asthma symptoms and 47,000 lost workdays.
The Trump administration is reversing the policy when the consequences of climate change — intense heat waves and stronger storms, for example — are becoming more obvious.

Extreme heat has baked much of the world this summer. July was the hottest month on record in the U.S., according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and many locations set all-time records. Overall, the three months from June through August were the warmest ever recorded for the contiguous United States.

Last year was the third-hottest in modern history, according to Copernicus, the European Union’s climate monitoring service. The past 11 years have been the 11 warmest on record, Copernicus data shows.
The litigation over the new EPA policy changes could take years and might not resolve before President Donald Trump leaves office.

“These cases proceed relatively slowly in the courts of appeals,” said Meghan Greenfield, a partner at the law firm Jenner & Block who oversaw the EPA’s Supreme Court docket for rulemaking during the Biden administration. “It’s not clear to me at this point that this repeal, the one that’s being finalized today, will be before the Supreme Court by the end of this administration.”

title: Pennsylvania woman’s measles death shows risks to people with health problems
summary: The unvaccinated 40-year-old, who died Saturday, had asthma and lung disease, the county coroner’s office said. A test showed the woman tested positive for measles.
story: The Jefferson County, Pennsylvania coroner says he’s confirmed an “active measles infection” in a 40-year-old Pennsylvania woman who died Saturday morning. She also had ongoing lung problems, including asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, the coroner’s office said.
“She did have a pretty extensive medical history,” said Jason Stiver, chief deputy coroner and public relations officer for Jefferson County. “She was on oxygen 24/7.”
Monday evening, the coroner’s office said that a nasal swab taken from the woman upon her death tested positive for measles.
“The positive test result supports the determination that the decedent was suffering from an active measles infection at the time of death,” according to a press release from the coroner’s office.
The woman, Stiver said, was pronounced dead in her home just before 8 a.m. Saturday. She hadn’t been vaccinated against measles.
The woman had symptoms of measles, including a fever and the telltale rash, Stiver said, and was living in a house with other people who had the same measles symptoms.
She also had direct contact with another family member in a different household who had been “laboratory tested and confirmed” to have measles, Stiver said.

This is the third death in the state amid a surging outbreak of the virus. Two infants, according to the Lancaster County coroner, died last month of measles-related complications. One baby died at birth after his mother, also infected with measles, went into labor a month early.
As of Monday, 693 cases had been confirmed in the state this year, 99 of them in the last week alone.

The latest situation is a prime example of how the virus can be deadly in people with underlying health problems. Once measles begins circulating in the body, it can attack multiple organs, including the lungs and the heart. In very rare cases, an infection can result in a dangerous and almost always fatal brain condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, a decade later.

It also suggests that Pennsylvania’s outbreak is far worse than official case counts suggest. Historically, measles infections cause 1 to 2 deaths per 1,000 cases. Three deaths in a short period of time indicate the state may have as many as 3,000 cases. Many people, experts say, don’t get tested.

News of the latest death comes amid an ongoing political back-and-forth between Pennsylvania and federal health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn’t acknowledged the measles deaths in the state.

A spokesperson from the state Health Department told NBC News the agency informed the CDC on Monday morning that it was investigating the death in Jefferson County, which a CDC spokesperson confirmed.
The CDC’s director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, said in a statement that, unlike other states with outbreaks, Pennsylvania hadn’t requested the CDC’s assistance in its ongoing measles outbreak.

The Pennsylvania Health Department “maintains a strong working relationship with the professional staff at the CDC, which includes regular meetings, and we will continue to evaluate any additional CDC support as this outbreak continues,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.
The U.S. is experiencing its largest measles outbreak since 1991, with 3,294 confirmed cases this year, according to the CDC.

In addition to the people who have died in Pennsylvania, three others died of complications related to measles in 2025. One was an adult in New Mexico. Two young girls died in Texas in its massive outbreak, which ultimately spread to at least 762 people.

title: Trump vowed to identify more of the donors to his ballroom project. That hasn’t happened yet.
summary: The White House released a list of some contributors in October but hasn’t elaborated in nearly a year as the cost of the project has ballooned.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly promised to share the names of the private donors funding his massive ballroom. But nearly a year after he tore down the White House’s East Wing to make room for the roughly $400 million project, only a partial list of contributors has been made public.
“I’ll give you names,” Trump said in the Oval Office just last month. “In fact, I wanted to put them out today, but we got a little busy.”

The White House released in October an initial list of 37 donors whom Trump feted at an East Room dinner event to “Establish the Magnificent White House Ballroom,” an official said at the time. The list included corporations, individuals and family foundations. Among them were Comcast Corp., NBCUniversal’s parent company; Apple; Amazon; Microsoft; Google; Meta; Lockheed Martin; and Coinbase.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The White House did not disclose how much each company donated or whether they made additional donations after the initial 2025 dinner. Since then, no additional donors have been made public by the Trump administration, though a few have acknowledged donations on their own, including Nvidia and Vantive Healthcare.
Democrats in Congress and government transparency groups have raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest and federal favoritism toward anonymous donors.

Trump initially estimated that the ballroom would cost $200 million, paid for entirely by donors, including himself, though it is not clear if he has contributed to the project. Since then, the price tag has risen to at least $400 million, according to the administration’s latest estimate, with additional taxpayer funding going to security improvements for the White House writ large, which could include the ballroom site.
The White House declined to comment for this article.

The donations are funneled through the Trust for the National Mall, a tax-exempt nonprofit organization, which did not respond to a request for comment. Individual and corporate donors can typically deduct the amount they contributed from their federal income taxes. A person raising money for the ballroom told NBC News last year that they were asking for donations of $2.5 million to $5 million and that the deduction is one reason people choose to give.

Last month, congressional Democrats pushed for more information about the donors, saying the public has a right to know if entities are making donations to a project Trump has personally prioritized in order to seek benefits from his administration, an indication they will likely probe the project if they win back the House in November’s midterm elections. The House Natural Resources Committee and the Oversight and Investigations Subcommittee have requested more information from the National Park Service and Trust for the National Mall.
“The Trust may have been used as a vehicle for billionaires and corporations to curry political favor with the Trump administration in a potential violation of federal law,” the lawmakers wrote.

Democratic senators, including Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, have also pressed the donors directly for more details, as groups like Public Citizen, a progressive consumer rights advocacy group, have raised questions about possible conflicts of interest.

Over half of the publicly identified corporate ballroom donors, 14 out of 27, have received new or bigger government contracts since October, totaling over $50 billion, according to Public Citizen’s analysis. The group also found that 16 of the 27 donors are either currently facing federal enforcement actions or have had them suspended by the Trump administration.

The president has insisted the ballroom and military complex are essential for national security, a case the Trump administration made to several lower courts before going to the Supreme Court to justify its ongoing construction. In late August, the justices ruled 5-4 to allow it to move forward.
Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court’s three liberals in dissent, writing that the plans are “likely unlawful.”

Trump has insisted that no taxpayer money is being used for the ballroom, but at least $300 million of Secret Service funds were redirected to the White House for security enhancements to the overall complex, according to Office of Management and Budget documents, which could apply to the ballroom, as well. Republicans in May suggested using $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to secure the ballroom project, but that funding did not get off the ground.

Trump has continued to make a security case for the ballroom, particularly after a gunman attempted to gain access to the White House Correspondents’ Dinner earlier this year. Such events could take place in a much more secure ballroom on the White House campus in the future, he’s suggested, though the event is independent and hosted by an outside nonprofit of journalists.
“The people that are opposing the ballroom are people that, in my opinion, are very disloyal to our country, very, very disloyal to our country,” Trump told reporters last month.
The Trump administration says the project is about 65% complete, with 250 crew members working 20 hours a day to get it done. It’s expected to be completed by the summer of 2028.
“It’s a gift from great patriots of this country,” Trump said in August.

title: Chicago police officer suspended after hurling insult at and unlawfully searching a pedestrian, review finds
summary: The Civilian Office of Police Accountability said body-camera video verified that one of the officers told the pair they were stopped because they were “ugly as f---.”
story: A Chicago police officer unlawfully stopped and searched a student walking home from the bus, telling him and the person he was with that they were targeted because they were “ugly as f---,” according to findings released by a watchdog group.

The Civilian Office of Police Accountability (COPA) reviewed and analyzed body-camera video of the incident that unfolded after three officers stopped a male and a female around 1:50 p.m. on Dec. 10, 2024.

Police Officer Oscar Furlan and two colleagues were patrolling the Jackson Park neighborhood in an unmarked Chicago Police Department vehicle when they spotted the individuals who later reported the troubling encounter to COPA.
Furlan at first told the male that he was stopped because he looked “like you got some s--- on you.”
The pair, whose names and ages were redacted from the COPA report, told officers that they were on the way home from school and had just gotten off the bus, the report, released on Wednesday, says.

COPA said that during its investigation the officers “stated they stopped [the male] because they were in a high crime area, they observed [the male] walking with his hands in his pockets” and that he ignored one of the officers “when she asked him to remove his hands from his pockets.”
The male told the officers his hands were in his pockets because he was cold. The report said the temperature that day in Chicago was in the 30s.
Furlan told the COPA investigators that the male in question “had his hands in his pocket, acting like he was clutching something tight towards his waist or holding onto something tight.”
The male was briefly detained and patted down. Police did not find any contraband or weapons on him, and they were allowed to leave.
As they were walking away, Furlan hurled an insult at the pair.
“We stopped you because you are ugly as f---,” Furlan said.

COPA determined that the male was stopped and searched without justification. The group found that while the male tried to ignore the stop request, “nothing in his behavior suggested that he was dangerous or presented a danger of attack.”
The officers also failed to properly document the stop, COPA found.
Furlan violated Chicago Police Department policies that prohibit officers from disrespecting and insulting members of the public, according to the report.
COPA recommended a 10-day suspension for Furlan and for him to be retrained on “professionalism, investigatory stops, protective pat-downs, and related reporting requirements.”
The Chicago Police Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Furlan did not respond to a request for comment.

The department agreed to suspend Furlan for five days. One of the other officers involved was expected to get a three-day suspension and the third was due to get reprimanded, the Chicago Police Department confirmed in an Aug. 11 letter to COPA. The department also agreed to put the officers through “investigatory stop, pat-down, and professionalism training,” the letter went on to say.

title: Pentagon inspector general says Iran war has led to a shortfall of U.S. munitions
summary: It’s the first public report on the ongoing war started Feb. 28 by the U.S. and Israel.
story: WASHINGTON — The Defense Department’s inspector general released its first report on the war with Iran on Monday, saying the conflict has resulted in a shortfall of U.S. munitions and “bottlenecks” in supply chains as the Trump administration works to replenish weaponry.

“To mitigate these constraints,” the report said, the Pentagon is “working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times, and to stockpile critical materials, components, and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency.”
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has denied reports that the U.S. is running low on munitions.

President Donald Trump said Monday on Truth Social that the U.S. is “producing more Exquisite and Elite Weapons than at any time in our History. They are being delivered on a daily basis to our Forces in the Middle East and beyond.”
Two weeks ago, Trump posted that the U.S. had “virtually unlimited” amounts of ammunition and lashed out at reports of munitions shortfalls.

The congressionally mandated report covers from the start of the war on Feb. 28 through June 30. It is one of the first public accountings from any government agency detailing the cost, scope and scale of the U.S.- and Israel-led conflict to the U.S. military, the State Department and other agencies. It follows reports of low morale among U.S. troops deployed to the Middle East, a depleting stockpile of key munitions and extensive damage to American military and intelligence assets in the region.
Among the findings, the report provides one of the first government confirmations that Iran targeted the U.S. Navy’s main logistics hub in the region, in Bahrain, with drones and ballistic missiles.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report.

It does not address what was most likely a U.S. strike on an elementary school in Iran during the initial hours of strikes. The military has yet to release an internal investigation into the bombing; NBC News reported in June that a report was being finalized.
The watchdog’s report details the damage to military equipment, aircraft and other materiel over the first four months of the war, including the destruction of at least 30 large U.S. drones.

It says the war with Iran has cost roughly $33.4 billion, which does not account for repairing damaged facilities. It does include $22.3 billion in expended munitions, $3.7 billion for equipment losses and $7.4 billion in other expenditures.

NBC News reported in July that the war had so far cost $80 billion to $100 billion, according to three U.S. officials and three people familiar with the internal cost estimates. The Pentagon publicly said in July that the war cost $37.5 billion. Its estimate does not include the cost of replacing aircraft, repairing U.S. bases and replenishing critical weaponry.
Trump initially said the war would last for only weeks. But over the weekend, he said it might not end until “right after” November’s midterm elections or perhaps before.
The report also finds that the war has displaced more than 20,000 U.S. military and diplomatic personnel, who were relocated at the outset of the conflict and in the days and weeks after.

Most medical evaluations of injured U.S. forces were carried out on the ground, some by local ambulances, and the patients were taken to local treatment facilities because airlift capabilities had been moved because of concerns.
And U.S. forces flew as many as 5,000 flights from European bases in support of the war, though Trump has bitterly complained that European allies have not done enough to help support the war.

The report catalogs some of the damage to U.S. aircraft and other military gear, as well as some of the American bases in the region. Aircraft costs, for example, include destruction or extensive damage to four F-15E jet fighters, an F-35A Joint Strike Fighter and an A-10 Warthog, which was also destroyed, according to the report. Twelve KC-135 refuelers and nine other aircraft were also destroyed, the report says. More than 30 MQ-9 drones had also been destroyed as of June, according to the report, citing the Congressional Research Service.

The State Department sustained more than $208 million in damage in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — according to the report. That includes $184 million in damages to “diplomatic facilities” and $25 million more due to delays in construction projects, the report says.

The damage Iran inflicted on U.S. military bases had been far more extensive than is publicly known, NBC News reported in April. Iran also caused more damage to America’s intelligence and surveillance assets in the region than U.S. spy agencies have ever endured, and it is estimated to cost billions to repair, NBC News reported last month.
The report does not touch on the morale of U.S. troops who have been deployed as part of the war effort.

In recent weeks, concerns about deteriorating conditions for troops serving in the Middle East on the USS Abraham Lincoln during an extended deployment had escalated, and the Pentagon announced it was replacing the aircraft carrier.
The Lincoln is en route back to its port in San Diego after a stop in Thailand.

Television fans found out which stars came out victorious in tough categories like outstanding lead actress in a drama series and outstanding lead actor in a comedy series. Follow live coverage of the 2026 Emmys
